Coarse Grains

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT WITH RESPECT TO COARSE GRAINS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. J. A. MaeKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last I intimated to the house that I expected to be able to make a statement shortly with respect to the coarse grain situation. This matter has been fully considered and I wish to make a statement outlining the government's policy.
Members of this house will recall that the government's programme for the 1942-43 crop year was a programme designed to stimulate the production of coarse grains and to remove any fear of a decline, in the. prices of these grains as a result of increased production. Minimum basic prices of forty-five cents for oats and sixty cent} for barley were guaranteed, with the Canadian wheat board instructed to purchase in the event that the market declined to these floor prices. At times last autumn the board had to purchase both oats and barley in order to prevent a further decline in prices, and it was only because of the development of a heavy feed grain demand from the United States and difficulty in making delivery that this situation has not continued. It was clearly stated last year that the ceiling prices of 51i cents on oats and 64| cents on barley would be maintained, and this part of the coarse grains programme has effectively contributed to the maintenance of our live stock programme.
Since early in February, Winnipeg prices for oats and barley have been at or close to ceiling levels. In the meantime, United States grain markets have been advancing, and the difference between our prices and United States prices has widened considerably. The government were naturally concerned about finding a means to enable the western farmer to benefit from the United States market, and at the same time to maintain those price controls in the domestic market which are a part of national policy.
Another problem arising from these circumstances which had to be considered by the government was the fact that exporters of Canadian feed grains were placed in a position to obtain more than a normal margin, had export permits been freely issued. The government is naturally concerned that the full American price less transportation, duty, and forwarding costs be returned to the western producer.
The price ceilings on coarse grains in the Winnipeg market were imposed as part of our national price control policy, and were
based on the highest prices recorded during the base period. With the price control policy in effect, it is important that domestic feeders who purchase coarse grains will be able to keep their feed costs in proper line with the prices received for the bacon, beef, dairy and poultry products which they are producing and upon which there are various ceiling and contract prices, in order to meet the needs of the United Kingdom and our own domestic food requirements. Without the ceiling protection, feed prices could and might rise to a level which would prejudice the effective prosecution of our extensive and vital live stock programme.
It is of the greatest importance that any action taken at this time should not disturb the basis of live stock production. It is the considered view of the government, therefore, that the ceilings on oats and barley in the Winnipeg market must be retained. To the extent that coarse grains can be exported at prices above our ceiling levels, the government have sought to develop a workable basis which would give producers who sell coarse grains the advantage of any higher export prices on that portion of the total coarse grain marketings which go into export.
With this principle in mind the government are instructing the Canadian wheat board to charge an equalization fee on the issuance of export permits to exporters of Canadian oats and barley. The equalization fee will, as nearly as possible, represent the difference between Canadian prices and United States prices, less transportation costs, United States import duty and forwarding costs, and with allowance for exchange. The equalization fee will not be fixed but will vary in accordance with the United States prices as compared with Canadian prices.
The Canadian wheat board will set up two special funds into which equalization fees for oats and barley, respectively, will be paid. These funds, in turn, will be distributed at the end of the crop year on a pro rata basis to the growers who have delivered these grains since March 31. Naturally, the amount in either of these funds for distribution to farmers will depend upon the future margin between Canadian and United States prices and upon the volume of exports.
By the method I have just outlined, the growers who sell their coarse grains will receive, in effect, a combined price, which reflects the ceiling price on that portion of their sales which has been disposed of in the domestic market, and the export price on that portion which has been disposed of in the export market.
Coarse Grains

This policy will, I trust, commend itself both to the producers and the domestic buyers of coarse grains as being fair. It assures the continuation of Canada's food production programme in so far as meat, dairy and poultry products are concerned. In regard to export markets the government are determined that the full advantage of these markets will be shared by producers marketing oats and barley on any surplus of these grains available for export, after the domestic requirements needed to maintain a full live stock production are adequately met.
The clear object of these arrangements in regard to oats and barley is to ensure that the full export returns for these grains should go to the producer and should not accrue to the exporter or to the purchaser abroad. The situation in respect of rye is different. Out of a western crop of 23 million bushels, only about one million bushels are disposed of commercially within Canada, and a considerable part of that is for uses for which other grains are equally good. The government's object can therefore be achieved most easily in the case of rye, having regard particularly to economy and facility of administration, by permitting the price of rye to conform to export prices rather than by adopting the system of an equalization fee for the sake of a small and relatively nonessential portion of the crop.
I am, therefore, authorized on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, to announce that he has discussed this matter with the wartime prices and trade board and that the ceiling on rye will be removed as soon as the Canadian wheat board has completed a survey of the market po*sition in that grain. At the present time there is very little difference between rye prices in Canada and the United States after taking into account transportation costs, forwarding costs, exchange and duty. On this basis it would not appear that there would be any substantial rise in Canadian prices of rye. If a substantial rise in price does take place, however, there will of course be a corresponding increase in the cost of rye to Canadian consumers. As already explained, the quantity of rye disposed of commercially within Canada is very small, and it is clear that most of what is consumed could be readily replaced by other grains. There may be a few cases of essential use, however, and the Minister of Finance has directed the wartime prices and trade board to make a thorough investigation of any claims that arise and to make appropriate arrangements for absorbing part or all of these increased costs where it can be shown that the consumption of this grain is essential.

PRIVILEGE-Mr. DOUGLAS
On the orders of the day:

I desire to raise a question affecting the privileges of this house. On March 17 an order of the house was passed for a return of all correspondence, memoranda and other documents received from the advisory committee to the wheat board, agricultural and cooperative organizations, with reference to the marketing of the 1943-44 crop. When that was passed the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, at page 1324 of Hansard:
I assume that this motion refers to correspondence, memoranda and other documents addressed by the organizations mentioned to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have no objection to the passing of the motion subject to the withholding of any confidential or privileged documents.
The minister made no specific statement as to considering any of the documents mentioned in the motion as being privileged; he was merely making a general statement that the motion would be passed subject to the reservation of withholding any documents which might be considered privileged. That order was brought down in sessional paper No. 76B on April 1. It says this:
1. Memoranda and other documents received from the advisory committee to the wheat board are considered privileged documents.
I submit that the advisory committee to the wheat board is not a branch of the government; these are not officials of a department reporting to a minister, they are private citizens, representing the producers, the grain trade, the milling trade and the

line elevators, who have been asked to act on a committee to make reports from time to time to the wheat board. I claim therefore that the reports of this committee cannot be considered in any sense privileged. If I remember correctly, at a previous session the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) quoted from one of the reports* of the advisory committee to the wheat board. The persons acting on this committee are private individuals representing a certain class of the people of Canada. The people of Canada have a right to know what recommendations are being made by the members of this committee, and also to what extent their recommendations are being implemented by the government. I therefore protest against the withholding of these reports. I believe that such an action is a violation of the privileges of this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Upon the point of privilege raised by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) which has been answered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), I think members of parliament should be very careful not to build a fence around the whole matter of information so far as the government is concerned. I am not familiar with this particular question, nor have I been able to give it attention except when hearing what the hon. member for Weyburn has just said. But it seems significant to me, first of all, that yesterday we had a battle on the floor of the house with respect to the matter of the production of correspondence between the dominion and the provincial governments; further, from time to time ministers, heads of departments, decline to answer questions in this chamber because in their opinion to answer them is not in the public interest; and now comes this further evidence of a trend which, I think, is peculiarly unfortunate at this time when the public are anxious to find out what is going on behind the scenes in parliament and in government.
It seems to me that this issue transcends many of the matters we have discussed here,

Privilege-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
because it goes much farther than an ordinary question of privilege. If this practice is allowed to develop, those who sit on the opposition benches are likely to be confronted with difficulties more substantial than those which we encounter now.
I would urge upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with all the vehemence at my command, that he reconsider and reverse the decision he has just announced with respect to the bringing down of information such as has been referred to this afternoon. It indicates a dangerous growth and a serious practice. An important principle is involved, and we members of the opposition would be derelict in our duty if we did not see to it that this tendency shall not be allowed to continue, to the detriment, if I may say so, of intelligent criticism of the government's war effort.

May I say a word on behalf of our group? I do not think it is the duty of this house to ask a minister to reconsider 'his decision; it is the duty of the house to take such a decision itself. In my opinion we are getting away entirely from the basis upon which the institution of parliamentary government rests. It has always been understood that the only privileged documents are documents passing between governments dealing with affairs of state; and when I speak of "governments" I mean sovereign governments ruling nations. From time to time we are faced with refusals to grant the tabling of documents which will enable this house to judge of what is going on. If the advice of the advisory committee to a board set up by a statute of this parliament cannot be tabled in this house, we are, I think being denied rights which the house should have. If the gentlemen who comprise that committee are making reports which they do not wish the people they represent to see, that is. subversive of the public interest and the time has come when we should get a clear understanding. My reading of constitutional procedure is that this is a sovereign parliament, that the government is merely an executive arm responsible to this house, and that the government and the minister have no right to constitute themselves a supervisory body to decide what this house shall know and what it shall not know. Parliament itself, not the ministers, ought to take cognizance of what is going on and decide the procedure in the light of the traditions of British parliamentary institutions.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct attention to a matter which I consider to be of the greatest importance; I

refer to labour conditions in Canada. This question has cropped up every now and then during the debates which have taken place since the opening of this session. But a speech made in Montreal yesterday by one whom I would call a government employee or government official, cannot, I think, be allowed to pass without some comment. In the few minutes of the time of the house I shall take up I shall place before hon. members the .position of the workers, as it was not placed before the select audience which was addressed by Mr. Justice McTague yesterday. On the front page of to-day's issue of the Montreal Gazette there is an editorial dealing with that speech; and I am quite convinced that whenever the Montreal Gazette carries a front page editorial on matters affecting labour, then labour had better look out because it bodes no good to labour.
Before going on with the comment I want to make on this speech let me say that I have had occasion to refer to Mr. Justice McTague in not an unkind way in this house on previous occasions, notably when he was made chairman of the national war labour board. I considered then and I consider now that he is preeminent in his understanding of the questions with which he has to deal and is progressive and generous in regard to labour matters. I think I can say the same in regard to the labour representative on that board. I cannot say anything in -regard to the third member, because I do not know him; consequently I am not saying anything either for or against him.
I am going to quote some excerpts from the speech made yesterday by the chairman of the national war labour board which in my opinion are very good, but I question the right or even the wisdom, if you like, of a person in his position making a speech of this kind particularly at this time, because the chairman of the national war labour board is in a certain sense a judge. In referring to the board at the time it was set up the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said it was the intention to build up a labour jurisprudence so that the matters referred to it might be dealt with from a juridical point of view. Mr. Justice McTague said:
It is my view that industry's day of being paternalistic and deciding by direct and indirect means just what type of union it will deal with, has long gone by or else is going by so rapidly that only he who is afflicted with a mote or a beam or a combination of both, can fail to see it.
Really it is this combination of the mote and the beam, this opposition to trade unionism, that is at the bottom of most of our labour troubles. I noticed in the same issue of the Gazette a news item dated

War Labour Board
Hamilton, April 5. It referred to a letter signed by fifty-six industrial firms in the city of Hamilton opposing the collective bargaining bill now before the legislature of Ontario. Here we have the largest industrial province in Canada, the most important industrial province, without any labour legislation recognizing and regulating trade unions. Then when an attempt is made to provide that kind of legislation we have all- or not all; it would not be fair to say that -at least a majority of the employers of labour opposing a measure which is long overdue in a province so important industrially as is Ontario. I fully agree with the chairman on that point. He says further:
The present situation-by that I mean now- places a grave responsibility on industry, on labour and on government. All must think in terms of fundamentals. Either we are fighting and all fighting in this war for our very existence, or we are not. Either the war we are in is a total war, or it is not.
I agree -with that. But before I sit down-I shall show this house that one of the difficulties is that labour is not at all convinced that in its operations industry is carrying on an all-out war effort at this time.
With the next item I quote from the chairman's speech I do not agree at all. In the select audience of employers that he was addressing, he went out of his way to attack certain persons unnamed, which attack, because of the position he holds was quite unjustified. If the chairman of the board can go out and make speeches of this kind, what is to prevent other members of the board from doing the same? And if that kind of thing is indulged in, what sort of labour board are we to have? He said:
Demagogues, whether union organizers or politicians, must consider with care and caution the forces of mob rule which they may be letting loose in this country-letting loose not only on the country but on themselves as well.
Let me point out that according to the chairman of the national war labour board all demagogues are either politicians or union organizers; there are no demagogues in industry; there are no industrial demagogues in Canada. From the point of view of the chairman of the national war labour board there may be no industrial demagogues in Canada, but there are many industrial reactionaries, which, in my opinion, are worse than demagogues. They would put the lid on progress and by the very action of trying to prevent orderly progress they make the social upheavals the chairman referred to inevitable. The utterances of demagogues can have no appeal unless the material conditions of discontent are there already. The chairman went on to say:
72537-119}
There can be no excuse in times of war for strikes, if there is lawful means available for obtaining the justice sought. It must be recognized by governments that these outbreaks cannot continue to be regarded as isolated events, they are not isolated. They cannot be kept isolated.
If they take place-
Note this:
-they must be stamped out with the same ruthlessness with which they are promoted.
That is very strong language for an employee of the government to use in advising the government.
I will connect with that another statement in the speech:
Even an unusually patient government will have to take drastic action if more of these events occur. When that time comes-and it must come if we have not changed the morali code and made the illegal the legal-people will be hurt, and seriously hurt. Blood has run before in this country in strikes.
I want to say to this house that that is a speech that should not have, been made, particularly at a time when the board of which Mr. Justice McTague is chairman has made a decision which has not yet been accepted by those whom it affects. What effect is that speech going to have? It can have none other than to inflame all the passions and prejudices human nature is heir to and that a man in the chairman's position should try to allay.
Labour may have legal means to attain its ends. But these legal means move very slowly at times. Just to show what are some of the grievances which the workers in industry labour under let me read some passages from a document which was left with: me by some labour men only yesterday. This is a copy of a brief submitted to the Montreal members of parliament on February 27 by a delegation of trade unionists from Montreal war plants. I believe that all hon. members of this house should read this document; here is something of which they should take notice. The delegates make certain points very clear. They refer to-
The big number of layoffs taking place in the different war plants. Montreal Locomotive has laid off many hundreds from their big tank plant, said in some quarters to be the best equipped tank plant on the continent. Two. thousand men are being laid off from the tank plant of the Canadian Pacific Railway Angus shops; Robert Mitchell has also laid off hundreds, as did the Engineer Products not long: ago. The Cherrier plant of the Canadian Car and Foundry Company also laid off thousands of their munitions workers. Layoffs have become general. This is having the most demoralizing effect on the workers in general, who are asking for an explanation. So far no satisfactory explanation has been given.
I point out that workers are at this time particularly fearful of being laid off work..
War Labour Board

There are two reasons for that. Despite anything that any "demagogues", or reactionary industrialists may say, the workers in this country are anxious to win this war. That is one reason why they do not want to see plants standing idle at the same time as they are idle. But there is another reason. So many of our workers suffered so terribly from unemployment during the ten years prior to the war that they are frantic at the mere mention of anything that would even remotely resemble those terrible conditions in the hungry thirties. Paragraph 2 of the brief says:
Certain inequalities in wage rates as between those paid in the province of Quebec and the prevailing rates in other parts of the country. The laws are such as makes it well nigh impossible for the Quebec workers to aspire to equality with the workers in the west. This is greatly resented by the workers in our province. We believe that if proper adjustments were made, our war effort and national unity would be strengthened immeasurably.
I suggest that the chairman of the national war labour board should read and ponder paragraph 3:
The attitude of many employers which makes cooperation almost impossible. Here we refer to the fact that even in the face of recommendations by boards of conciliation there are still *employers who refuse to deal with their organized employees. Moreover, company unions are being set up, workers practically forced to join-
These are the people who oppose workers being compelled to join ordinary trade unions. They have no compunction, however, in making them join company unions. The brief *continues:
-and then tied up hand and foot through contracts drawn up under the Quebec Collective Agreements Act. At Arvida the company refuses to deal with the international union representing the great majority of the employees, and are actively supported by the Quebec government.
4.	Discrimination is rampant. Workers are fired for union activity. Young men are threatened with the draft for joining the union. Bribes are offered the workers to keep them from organizing. This is again very demoralizing, and should be prevented by severe penalties.
It is time that these matters were brought to the attention of the house. There was an opportunity for hon. members to do something before. Possibly if they had taken advantage of that opportunity something would have been done to further an understanding in respect of these questions affecting labour and employers.
Then, paragraph 5-and evidently Mr. Justice McTague, when he refers to legal means, has never heard of delays:
5.	The long delays attendant on having cases dealt with by the regional board are notorious.
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
Company unions can have wage adjustments made almost overnight, while bona fide unions have to fight for months to get fair treatment. We believe the board should sit continuously, and that in case of dissatisfaction with a decision, the unions should have the right of appeal to the national board.
I believe an amendment to the order in council now provides for that appeal.
I am not going to read the whole of this brief. There are some recommendations which in my view are quite reasonable, and should be considered. But what I wish to emphasize is that the facts-and they are facts-laid down in the brief can be duplicated in every industrial centre across Canada. I hold in my hand a letter received by myself only a few days ago from a worker in Hamilton. He had spoken to me verbally in the first instance, and I told him to put his complaint in writing so that I could bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Labour. He said that in certain industries in Hamilton-and I do not know whether it was so in this particular case-employees are laid off, not discharged. There is no work, and they are told when laid off that while there is no work they are still on the payroll. But when they apply for unemployment insurance they are told that they cannot be paid unemployment insurance benefits because they are still on. the payroll of the company. And, -worse, the employees of the selective service branch associate themselves with the company in carrying out this sort of discrimination.
I have a letter in my hand written on March 27. This one is from the president of local 2352 of the United Steelworkers of Canada, and, is in these words:
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed by the members of Local Union 2352 of the United Steelworkers of America, National Steel Car, Hamilton, to protest the continual lay-offs through cancellation or completion of War work. This procedure has placed employees of this plant on the street and speaks very distastefully of our war effort.
In May, 1942, the 4-5 shell shop was closed and in fact boarded up when the management found out that employees intended placing stickers on the idle machines reading "This machine is working for Hitler." This department has never operated only in rebuffing salvaged shells and approximately 10 per cent of the machines were actually used.
That means that ninety per cent were not used.
These machines are gathering dust and the employees have been transferred to other departments. But, production in other shell departments has been cut to one-third of the normal production and again the employees are losing time until placed.

War Labour Board
Improper planning and the malicious use of selective service has caused discontent to such a degree that a third strike at national may occur at any time although the union officers have done their utmost in cooperating fully with the management.
Two statements are frequently mentioned quite openly by the employees:
(a)	The management is provoking the employees to take militant action.
(b)	The directors of the company are endeavouring to cause "another Malton" condition so that the government will purchase this plant also.
In conclusion may I state that there is considerable heavy equipment for the fabrication of ship-plate, tanks, etc., that lies idle for periods of time in this plant. An investigation would prove this statement. The employees are desirous of producing in an all out effort to win this war.
Trusting you will give earnest consideration to this communication.
A great commotion is made about a strike, a lay-off by workers or by a certain amount of absenteeism; but I am satisfied that not one-tenth of the time lost through idle machinery, for some reason or another, is lost through strikes or absenteeism. To-day machinery' should not be idle. If we cannot produce tanks, or if tanks are not needed, then ships and more ships are needed. There is no reason in the world-with the exception, of course, of indifferent planning-why we should not be engaged in producing ships if other work is not available.
I do not- wish to delay the house longer in discussing this matter. I believe I have shown clearly that the workers have grievances, and that those grievances cannot be resolved by making unwise speeches to Canadian clubs or service clubs or organizations of any other kind. Manual workers do not belong to the Canadian club. They do not belong to it for two reasons; first, they cannot afford the admission fee, and second, they cannot take two or three hours off in the middle of the day to attend a luncheon and hear someone make a speech. They have useful work to do; they are necessary in keeping the country's production going. I say again that if the other members of the national war labour board are going to take advantage of the circumstances taken advantage of by the chairman, then the government had better disband this war labour board and set up another.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Let me say to my hon. friend that it takes considerable courage to be chairman of the national war labour board. It is much easier to make the kind of speech the hon. gentleman made this afternoon than it is to assume that responsibility. He talks of passion, but rarely have I seen more passion displayed in this house than was displayed this afternoon. If he does not use more judgment when he goes up and down this country than he used in this house this afternoon, there is reason for some of the industrial controversies we are having at the present moment.
My hon. friend spoke of the national board and the regional board. These boards are composed of members of labour organizations and others who represent the employers. In the provinces the chairman is the provincial minister of labour, whereas the national board is made up of Mr. Justice McTague as chairman and the other two members.
He spoke also of people being laid off, of there being a reduction at times in the industrial tempo of the country. If my hon. friend had had as much experience of war as some members of this House of Commons-I mean war in its practical sense-he would understand that it demands change. We are engaged in a mechanical war and we must be continually changing from one type of equipment to another, from one tank to another, from one aeroplane to another. This means retooling of plants in order to go on with the new production. It creates what in the old days we used to call technological unemployment. As an old trade unionist, I think he will agree with me when I say that years ago when we were always asking for an effective employment service we never expected we should have anything like the national selective service which we have at the present time. I think he will agree also that as compared with three years ago, the machinery in existence to-day for the transfer of workers from one industry to another is far greater than what we had contemplated in relation to the present war. The rules and regulations that have been put into force, the changes that have been created, are out of all proportion to what existed three years ago. In creating this machine we have had to deal with human beings, but I think it must be admitted that they are doing a very effective job, a much more effective job than I dared to hope they would be able to do.
My hon. friend read some letters. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that ever before
War Labour Board

I was in charge of the department the conciliation service was improved. When the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) was Minister of Labour, order in council 4020 was passed. I am not referring to
the Canadian club. I am talking about people who understand what makes the clock tick so far as labour legislation is concerned. I have always told my people that if we did not like the law we should try to have it changed through normal constitutional procedure. I think when the history of my generation is written it will be shown that we were somewhat successful in that regard.
Mention has been made of a patient government. Whether we. like it or not, the whole price ceiling is in jeopardy unless the national labour board and the regional boards are given that support by the people of this country which they richly deserve if they are to face up to the problem of inflation. I have always held this opinion, that when you go before a tribunal such as the national war labour board and they make a decision you are in duty bound to abide by that decision. I have never taken any other position since I have been connected with labour. I know that sometimes it is difficult to go back and explain the decision to your own people. In organizations people sometimes make promises which they know they cannot carry out, and my hon. friend knows that because he has been through all these things. Often the achievements have fallen short of the promises. But it is the duty of responsible leadership in this country, whether it be on the one side or on the other, to give to both sides the leadership to which they are entitled in the trying times through which we are passing. I still hold the opinion which I quoted yesterday of Sir Stafford Cripps, and I think it might be well if I quoted it again before I sit down. Speaking to

the people in the aeroplane plants in the United Kingdom after he had made a two-day tour of inspection, he said:

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the chance of keeping the ex-leader of the opposition away from the war, I am going to occupy a little of the time of the house this afternoon. The last time that this group raised a question in the house the leader of the opposition waxed eloquent on the theme that we were not getting on with the war, and then immediately afterwards he spent two hours discussing an extra cent postage stamp. So that I feel justified in occupying a little of the time of the house this afternoon.
The question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) is very pertinent to the war effort and to the future prosecution of the war. In fact I consider it the most important discussion in which this house could engage at the present time. I have stated on at least two occasions in this house that I consider the Department of Labour the most important war department in the government in that they have completely under their jurisdiction the organization and allocation of man-power and woman-power in this country. That is a job which requires considerable organization. In keeping the wheels of industry moving to produce the necessary war materials the departments of national defence and munitions and supply are merely the fifth wheel on the coach without the complete organization and functioning of the Department of Labour in its many ramifications.
The hon. member for Vancouver East this afternoon correctly pointed out that the new chairman of the national war labour board chose a very inopportune time to make the speech he did yesterday afternoon. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) quoted Sir Stafford Cripps with references to stoppages of work in war plants, and would lead the house to believe that the situation in the United Kingdom is analogous to that in Canada. I should like to make this observation, that in Great Britain labour is solidly organized. In Great Britain they still have the freedom of collective bargaining. They still do business with their employer. They have in practically every production plant in Great Britain workers' committees which are making their full contribution to the war effort. The trades union congress of Great Britain sits in with the cabinet in planning the war effort.
But in this country less than seventeen per cent of the workers who are eligible for membership in trades unions are in any kind of labour organization, and the result is that you have from coast to coast, in every industry necessary to the war effort a constant battle by the workers for the right to exercise that freedom of democracy which is enjoyed by the industrial workers of Great Britain, led by Bevin, Morrison, Attlee, Cripps, and other leaders who sit in with the cabinet safeguarding the rights of the average worker in Great Britain.

I said that less than seventeen per cent of our industrial workers who are eligible for membership in a trades union are in any labour organization. By and large ' the workers of Canada are engaged in a battle on the home front for the right to sit around a conference table with their employer. There are hundreds of valuable men engaged in the work of trades union organization to-day who could be doing an important job in the war effort were this work taken off their hands, were the government to decide that collective bargaining is the thing in Canada just as it is in Great Britain and in every other civilized country in the world. This is the only country in the civilized world that has not on its statute books trade union legislation.
But I did not get up this afternoon to go into that story again, because we have gone into it time and again. My purpose was to say that in every section of Canada there is in the minds of many people to-day a growing fear and a suspicion that instead of the Canadian people bending every effort towards making our maximum contribution to this war there are people in key positions behind the scenes who are pulling the thing back. Just stop and think for a moment how the industrial workers in this country have been treated during the past three years; and now after three years of war we are still talking about this question of the
War Labour Board

right of the worker to sit around the conference table with his employer and help him win the war. That is all they want to do.
The conciliation machinery of the labour department has not been improved since the war began. It is not as good as it was when the war broke out. Your conciliation machinery has been cluttered up. The taking of a strike vote is provided for by the conciliation machinery when no strike is intended; in order to get a board of conciliation the workers of a plant have to take a strike vote and decide by a majority that they are going on strike-something they do not intend at all. You sow in the minds of the workers the seeds of an idea that a strike is to take place; for the Minister of Labour knows that a large percentage of the workers who take part in that ballot have not the least conception of what the department's regulations are.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Yes; I say it was legal, and I will prove to the satisfaction of any fair-minded man in the chamber this afternoon, that it was; that the men in Montreal were forced into it.
I want to discuss the machinery as it functions. Take your stoppage in the basic industry of steel. Were the steel workers responsible for that? I say they were not. They utilized every piece of machinery provided by the Department of Labour. Not only that; away back in November, 1941, they started in on the job of getting a conciliation board to iron out their grievance. They followed it up week after week, month after month, and there was no redress. After conferences, and boards, and appeals to both regional and national boards, the whole matter finally culminated in a walk-out. It was not a strike. No official of the steel workers' union called it; it. was a matter of the steel workers at the Sault, Trenton and Sydney becoming disgusted after two years' delay. Having endeavoured to talk to everyone who had authority to settle the matter, they ultimately said "what is the use?" and walked off the plant.
The reason these walk-offs are occurring is that they seem to be the only means at the disposal of the men in the mines and the plants to get their grievances listened to. No attention is paid to anything else, so that finally they walk out. I say this after much experience in negotiations. I am, just as strongly as the minister or anyone else, in favour of amending the laws, and living up to them religiously. You will find that ninety-nine per cent of the trade unionists across this country, particularly of the leadership, take this attitude. They want to obey the laws and they will fight to improve the laws. But the time comes when they have to go back to their men. Month after month they have met the people who have the authority to settle their grievances, but without effect, and the men become disgusted and say, "There is no solution along this line; the only way to get an answer from these people is by a walk-out." After two years' delay that is what happened in the steel industry. It occurred because of the slowness of the machinery, because of lack of attention to the men's legitimate grievances by both regional and national boards.

War Labour Board
I am, afraid now of what may yet happen. You set up a new board, an industrial court, with three legal minds on that board. One of the first things they have done is to disregard completely one of the main representations of the steel workers, namely to make the steel industry of Canada a national industry so that the national war labour board could deal with it and settle the whole question at one time. Instead, it has been thrown back to the regions. It will be examined in Nova Scotia and in Ontario section by section, with different people taking different positions on the same question, with no uniformity in the matter of wages. So far as machinery is concerned we are right back where we were before. The only thing that has happened so far as that industrial court is concerned is that they have provided for an appeal from a regional board, to the national board. There is absolutely no improvement of machinery. The question is still unsettled after two years' negotiations. The matter started, of course, in April, 1941. At last, in August, 1942, a delegation was able to meet the war labour board. But the question is still unsettled. I think these fellows have been very patient and very reasonable.
Another point I would call to the attention of the Minister of Labour is that you cannot win this war with your mouth.
You are not going to win it in here, by arguing. I make no apologies for what I am saying, because if some attention is not paid to the matters which I am trying to bring to the attention of the government, I am just a little bit sceptical as to who is going to win this war. Personally, I want to win it; make no mistake about that; and I am not letting anyone, behind the scenes or otherwise, who is not particular about winning it pull any smoke screens so far as I am concerned. I am going to be quite frank in what I have to say.
I bring this to the attention of the Minister of Labour. The miners of Nova Scotia had a board under Mr. Justice McTague in March, 1941. The board handed down a decision to the effect that certain mechanical rates were to be levelled up to a prescribed wage. We are now in April, 1943, and the decision of that board has not been implemented yet; that money has not been paid. Mr. Justice McTague in his speech yesterday, as quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), says that decisions of the labour board will be enforced from now on. I hope they will be; and I hope that the rule is to work both ways. The miners of Nova Scotia have been
awaiting new negotiations, pending the settlement of the award made by the board back in 1941. I know that the union officials have found it difficult to keep their men in line; because at the district convention where they lay	down	their	policy	they	decidedthat until	that	matter was	taken	care ofthere should be no new negotiations. What happens in the miners' union is that on the first of April of each year, if there is not a signed agreement to take care of wages and conditions for the year following, internationally	they	down	tools.	They	did notdo it on	the first of	April;	they	are still
trying to get this matter settled with the company on the basis of the award which was granted by the board in March, 1941.
A word with respect to the Montreal tramways. It is important that hon. members should understand these things. The press has not given a true picture; for some reason of which I am ignorant, it has distorted the facts. I cannot understand the attitude of any newspaper which, in the light of our present situation, will deliberately garble and twist the facts to confuse the public and make an already bad situation much worse.
As I understand that situation, there was a union functioning; it had been there-

speechtext:
The ballot, the thing that precipitated the whole trouble and caused the walkout, also was read into Hansard by the Minister of Labour, as follows:
The national war labour board has just been changed. This change gives the negotiating committee the opportunity to make new attempts with regard to wages. Are you in favour of according the negotiating committee all the support it will need to undertake these attempts on your behalf?
If that ballot had been accepted and voted upon it would have meant that the negotiating committee, as set out in the agreement, would be the committee that would carry on further negotiations. The street railway men in Montreal objected to that ballot. On the 27th of the month the minority group made application to the management of the street railway to take a ballot; and you know it worked faster than any ballot I have ever seen, because they were ready to take the vote on the 29th, two days later, and it was in protest against taking that vote that these men walked off the job. The Minister of Labour set the matter out very clearly in Hansard; he used his office to try to offset that strike or walkout. He asked the men who were conducting that ballot to withdraw it, pending negotiations with the Department of Labour. It may be that this strike or walkout was illegal, in accordance with the interpretation that could be placed upon it by those of the legal profession, but personally I look at the justice of a ease in determining its legality. These men, in order to safeguard democracy, the right of negotiation and the right of majority rule, walked off the job. The minority group who precipitated the trouble in the taking of the ballot challenged the Minister of Labour when he asked them, in a very reasonable way, to withhold further action pending negotiations. The net result is that the matter has been settled and these men are back at work. I say that the right side

War Labour Board
*won, because in any case the majority should rule. That i3 my conception of it, and that is the side that won in the Montreal trouble.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: That could have been proven just as easily by a board of conciliation, without a strike.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, it could, and I say it never should have happened; but place the blame where it belongs. The small group who endeavoured to force that ballot on the large majority of the employees and against the wishes of the Department of Labour are the people who are in an illegal position, if there is any illegality attached to it.
What I am trying to point out to hon. members is the slowness of the machinery, the apparent lack of understanding on the part of many people who have to deal with the rank and file of the workers in ironing out these difficulties and arriving at a decision. Personally I cannot see any reason for it. I know that the great majority of the men and women of this country employed in industry, ninety-nine per cent of them, are fair and reasonable. It has been my experience that any time you are honest with them and tell them the truth about a thing, I do not care how bad it is, they will go all the way with you. When you are dishonest with them, when you lie to them, you run into difficulty and lose their confidence, and you find yourself in trouble all the time you remain in office.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is in his seat, and I should like to say a word to him with respect to the prosecution of the war effort. The crux of the whole war situation, in my opinion, is ships, and every available man and woman in Canada who can go into a shipyard and do anything in regard to the building of ships should be there. Before this debate closes I would like the Minister of Munitions and Supply to give this house some information with respect to the Angus shops. The situation there has been developing for some considerable time. By May 3 some 1,800 of the men employed in those shops will be out of work; there are some 200 idle now. These are skilled men, men who can take their place in many capacities in a shipbuilding yard-welders and men of various classifications. Two months ago they made representations to selective service with a view to putting the facilities of their organization at the disposal of selective service-and they have a good organization. Just a few days ago they were permitted to help selective service in the reallocation of their man-power.
There is no difficulty between the management and the employees in the Angus shops. There is complete cooperation. The union
communicated with the shipbuilding yards to find out whether their men could be utilized in any of the yards, and the answer they received was: No, there will be nothing in shipbuilding until late in the fall.
I should like the Minister of Munitions and Supply to explain this; it has never been explained to my satisfaction. The Valentine tank was being produced in the Angus shops. According to a statement I heard in the house the Valentine was considered the best tank that was sent to Russia. It is good in snow; it is good in the sand; it has a wide tread; it has a diesel engine as against the other tanks that have gasoline engines. When a tank with a gasoline engine is hit once by a shell or a bullet it becomes hot and blows up, but you can batter that diesel engine until further orders and it does not blow up. According to my information the Valentine tank is the best machine of the war; it is the thing with which to lead infantry. I want to know why it was taken out of production in Canada and some 1,800 men who could be used in the war effort left idle.
Another thing I should like the minister to say something about is Dominion Engineering Works in Montreal. That plant is capable of turning out one thousand guns a month, and our information is that at the present time it is turning out around four hundred. There is no night shift. Why is there not another shift working there? Why is that plant not working at its maximum.
The Angus shop people tell us also that during the time they were operating they were capable of turning out, I think it was, six tanks a day, but under orders from somewhere all they were producing was three. They were told that was the schedule and it could not be stepped up beyond that. The Minister of Labour says that war is a practical thing; I know a little about it too. I am not a flag-waver, but there are not many in this house who have seen more war than I did; I will let it go at that. We have to fight this war. These matters must be answered. We have to make full use of the man-power of this country. I have not met anyone in any industry who is not really anxious to do a job. The shoe is on the other foot; they are frustrated; they claim they are being held back. You get that story in every section of industry. We should' know something about it. It is one of the first things the Minister of Labour has to do, and: as Minister of Labour he owes a direct responsibility to the working people of this country. We should know in no uncertain terms.
War Labour Board

Those who are operating industry are being assisted. The government has been very generous to them in rebuilding and tooling plants and all that kind of thing. They are acquiring some wonderful machines, and they should be compelled immediately to do what is being done in Britain. According to a British white paper the trades union movement is considered one of the most essential factors in their war machine. I will give this to any one who wants to look at it. They would not be without it; they call the labour people in and consult them. They get a lot of work done in that way that you cannot hire dollar a year men to do, because the dollar a year men do not know that job in the way that men who live with it and grow up with it know it. They have not the contacts. If the Minister of Labour wants to do an efficient job-and I think he does-he should not permit anyone in this country to keep the machinery from him. If he had a collective bargaining organization in each plant, if production committees were in every plant and factory submitting reports about what is going on, you could plan ahead of time. You cannot buy that kind of organization. In the sections where it is operating they are doing that work themselves. But there is no coordination machinery; no one at tha.top who has power and authority is receiving these reports or doing anything about it.
I was in Sudbury two weeks ago. They are rrying to form a union. There are over four thousand men in the organization. There are two hundred stewards. These fellows tell me they are paying about $1,000 a year in order to belong to that union. Discrimination, wages cut; and they are still there fighting a little company union set up and sponsored by International Nickel. I wish the Minister of Labour could have sat in on that stewards' meeting with me. There were four hundred stewards reporting directly to the head of the union from every section of that mine on production, on what they are doing, what they could do and how they could improve things. That machinery is lying idle, rusting; the men are frustrated, cannot do anything. The answer to the troubles and problems of the minister so far as I am concerned is the organization of labour, its complete cooperation in these production committees. If I were in his place that is the fight I would be carrying on; I would not be on the auction block as he is to-day. The machinery necessary for him to work with is being withheld from him by the big industrialists of this country who do not want organization. That was well demonstrated when Elliott Little began to talk to the manufacturers' association; he was not on the inside very long.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
When I came into the house today I did not expect that this debate would come up. But as one of the members from Montreal, where the Montreal Tramways strike occurred, and as the member for the division where the company has its head office, I feel it my duty to say something on the subject.
I agree completely with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who preceded me, as to the importance of the subject of labour relations in Canada at the present time. I regret, however, that beyond that I find it impossible to follow them in the rest of their remarks. They criticized Mr. Justice McTague, chairman of the national war labour board, for having made a speech before the Canadian dub in Montreal yesterday. Mr. Justice McTague needs no words of commendation from me; everyone in Canada knows that there is no one who has a better reputation for being a true friend of labour, a true Canadian, or who is more trusted by labour than Mr. Justice McTague.
In the course of his speech he said:
The board which I head is prepared at all times to give each side full opportunity to present its case and will deliver its judgments on the merits of the case as it sees them, without labouring for technical ways out of difficulties. As far as we can do it, we shall not stand for any flouting of our judgments or the wringing of further concessions because of the agitation of pressure groups.
Demagogues, whether union organizers or politicians, must consider with care and caution the forces of mob rule wffiich they may be letting loose in this country-letting loose not only on the country but on themselves as well. The wise union leader who has been adhering and is adhering to a non-strike policy must receive support and not discouragement. Neither he nor his union can survive in a world where illegal action is rewarded with concessions.
I think I can say that I have been sympathetic -with the cause of Labour. I have worked for labour, attended labour meetings, in every way I can. On that account, because I have the true interest of labour at heart, I feel that in respect of this Montreal Tramways strike it is my duty to put before the house and the country my conviction, having some knowledge of the circumstances, that the strike was, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) said, illegal, unjustified and unwarranted. Because I take almost precisely the opposite view of that strike from that of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon, member for Cape Breton South,

War Labour Board
and because I feel the matter is important, and because it is already having repercussions right through the country, I propose, if I may, to -spend some minutes in discussing the facts surrounding the Montreal Tramways strike.
In the first place it should be remembered that in July, 1940, the Montreal Tramways Company negotiated an agreement with three representatives of the men, called the negotiating committee. Those representatives of the men had been selected by the men by secret ballot. The negotiating committee, working with the Montreal Tramways Company, worked out an agreement. That agreement, a long one, is public property, and is printed in the Quebec Official Gazette for September 21, 1940.
Before the agreement became law-because that is what happened-it was submitted to the men over a period of forty-eight hours, during which time copies were made available to them. Following that, another secret ballot was held, in which the men voted whether or not they would agree to the terms of the agreement. By an overwhelming majority they voted in favour of its adoption.
That agreement was then sent, as a collective labour agreement, to the minister of labour of Quebec who, in due course, published it in the Quebec Official Gazette, and gave notice that anyone who had any objection to make before it was declared to have the force of law should make such objection within the next thirty days. The Gazette reads:
Pursuant to the provisions of section 5 of the Collective Agreement Act, notice is hereby given by the honourable Edgar Rochette, Minister of Labour, that the Montreal Tramways Company has presented to him a request to the effect that the collective labour agreement entered into between:
On the one part:
The Montreal Tramways Company, hereinafter called the "company",
and, on the other part:
The association of the employees of the Montreal Tramways Company, hereinafter called the "negotiating committee", be rendered obligatory for the employer and the employees of the industry and the trades concerned according to the following conditions.
Then follow the paragraphs in the agreement, running to some 110 in number. As I have pointed out, the agreement then had the force of law, under the law of the province of Quebec, the Collective Labour Agreements Act, 4, Geo. VI, chapter 38. This was a collective labour agreement, having the force of law.
The agreement itself contained three provisions to which I shall refer the house. In
the first place, after providing for wage rates for the various classes of labour, and after making provisions for holidays and the like, the agreement states this, in paragraph 107:
All conditions of this agreement, except those applicable to wages and holidays, shall remain in force for at least three years, or for the duration of the war, whichever period is longer.
The agreement was for three years or for the duration of the war.
Then, in paragraph 109, this was expressly stated:
The negotiating committee referred to in this agreement, consisting of Messrs. Elphege Beaudoin, Raoul Trepanier and Osias Neveu, will continue in office during the life of the agreement.
Later on in that paragraph provision was-made for the replacement of any member of the negotiating committee who might cease to act. In accordance with that provision Raoul Trepanier, upon being appointed to the Department of Labour, was replaced by the action of the other two members, and ceased to act for the committee-contrary to the impression given by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Would the hon. member tell us by whom Mr. Trepanier was replaced? According to this clause in the agreement he was not replaced.
Mr. CLAXTO'N: The agreement was made in 1940, and paragraph 109 provides for the method of replacement, which was followed out in this instance. Who replaced him escapes my memory at the moment, but I can give my hon. friends the name immediately after the adjournment of this sitting. He was replaced. He was not acting at the time this, matter in dispute arose.
In addition, the contract provided for a bonus, to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred. That was provided for in paragraph 110. The provision, which I shall summarize, is that 25 per cent of the gross income of the company over $15,000,000 in any year, ending June 30. shall be paid to the employees of the company who have been in its service for one year, and who are earning 82,500 or less. That paragraph was in full force and effect until! the dominion government passed order in-, council 7440.
The negotiating committee for the employees of the Montreal Tramways Company-made application to the Quebec regional war labour board for a declaration that this bonus, of 25 per cent of the gross profits over S15,000,000 as provided for under the agreement, should be paid to them. The
War Labour Board

Quebec regional war labour board held a number of hearings. Briefs were filed and, ultimately, on June 2, 1942, the board gave a decision stating, if I may summarize it, that the provision with regard to the bonus could not operate in conflict with the wageceiling provisions; that the bonus had to be paid by the company only up to November 15, 1941; that it could be paid at the company's -option up to January 1, 1942, and that it -could not be paid after that date. In lieu of the bonus there was to be a cost-of-living ibonus.
Pursuant to that order not only did the company pay what it had to pay in accordance with the decision, namely, the proportion of the bonus for the period up to November 15, 1941, but it went on and voluntarily paid what might be payable up to January 1, 1942. Then it had to stop because the regional war labour board, presumably acting in accordance with the authority conferred upon it by the government, had given the direction that this bonus was not payable, but that -cost-of-living bonus was payable. Since then the company has been paying the cost-of-living bonus, which at the present time I think is $2.40 a week.
