speechtext:
It may be. Those applications were made. Certainly one was rejected, and I think one or two more as well. This brings us to the beginning of January 1943, when the brotherhood began to correspond with the company and to represent to the company that it should replace the negotiating committee as the negotiating committee. It represented in correspondence which was made available to the press that it had the support of the majority of the men, and it urged that it should replace the negotiating committee as the negotiating committee. Further correspondence ensued, and then on March 2, 1943, the brotherhood, that is the union on the way in, made application for a board under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The conclusion of that application was that they be recognized as the negotiating committee to represent the men,
Whether or not there was a strike vote before that application was made escapes my memory. There should have been a strike vote in order to justify it under the act, but my impression is that there was no vote taken at that time. In any event the application was made. The brotherhood recognized that the proper way to proceed was to make an application to the minister for a board under the act. It did so and a board was appointed. The board sat in Montreal on Wednesday, March 24, and heard the brotherhood, the A. F. of L. union and the company representatives, and then stated that a report would be made to the minister. That report could not have reached the minister before Thursday or Friday. When it did reach him I do not know, but presumably it must have reached him on Friday or Saturday. Then occurred the incident to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred. The A.F.of L. union asked that a ballot should be taken of all employees in order to obtain a vote of confidence. At that time the question was pro-

War Labour Board
pounded in the form which has already been put on Hansard by the Minister of Labour. The A. F. of L. union or the negotiating committee asked the company if this ballot could be taken on the company's premises, and I think the company granted that permission on Saturday. That is the course of events up to the time when the word "strike" was first mentioned.
On Saturday afternoon the brotherhood, acting through its president, Mr. A. R. Mosher, said that if this ballot was proceeded with, there would be a strike on Monday. The matter reached the attention of the minister or his officers on Sunday, and the minister sent telegrams, which are already on record, to Mr. Mosher of the brotherhood; to Mr. Beaudoin, president of the A.F. of L. union, and to Mr. Blair, general manager of the company. In the telegrams to Beaudoin and Blair the minister urged that the ballot be called off and said that a board would be held to decide the matter of jurisdiction. In the telegram to Mr. Mosher he urged that the strike be called off and characterized it as being illegal, or used words to that effect. He also suggested that a board would be held to decide the matter of jurisdiction. As the Minister of Labour has said in the house, the formula selected by him and urged by him on the three parties was the right formula to end this dispute. Unfortunately all three parties replied in the negative or not at all to the telegrams. So that the strike began on Monday morning.
I have lived in Montreal all my life, and the faces of a great number of the striking motormen and conductors have been familiar to me for thirty-five or forty years. Many of them are in the category of friends. A great number of them have many gold stripes on their sleeves, each representing five years of service. I think it is fair to say that during the terrible conditions of this winter, despite tremendous congestion they rendered a fine service. When the strike occurred the men who were supporting the brotherhood were kept in the Atwater market, and of course their officers negotiated for them.
Montreal was almost totally unprepared for this strike, but from the beginning the people took it exceedingly well. They walked long distances to work. One of my staff walked over five miles to her work and this was characteristic of many of the population. There was a spirit of camaraderie. By late Monday afternoon many of the munitions plants had organized their own transportation services. All through, the spirit and organization of the people of Montreal was worthy of all admiration.
But the fact is that this strike interfered with the ordinary passage of a million passengers a day. A million passengers a day were inconvenienced and put to no end of trouble, some to distress. Of this number at least 100,000 were engaged in munitions work. One munition plant is reported not to have been able to do any work that day. Newspapers reported that some sixteen of the principal munitions plants in Montreal were working throughout the day at a capacity of from fifty to eighty or ninety per cent. There can be no doubt that the strike affected the production of munitions by those plants in Montreal.
On Tuesday, Mr. Goldenberg, sent by the minister, arrived in Montreal and that morning got in touch with the various interests. The next morning, Wednesday, he announced that a settlement had been arrived at. The settlement was virtually this, that the brotherhood was recognized as having the right to nominate the negotiating committee. In other words, precisely what the brotherhood had sought from the board appointed under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, precisely what had been under discussion before that board on the previous Wednesday, was obtained by this union by reason of this strike, which was stated by the minister to be illegal.
Therefore it seemed that if you wanted to obtain what you wanted, you should ask for a board, issue an ultimatum, have a strike declared illegal, hold up a million passengers, hold up 100,000 munition workers, cause distress and inconvenience, have the Minister of Labour declare the strike to be illegal, unjustified and unwarranted, and then on Wednesday get precisely what you wanted.
I take a serious view of this situation, equally serious with that of the members who spoke, but for directly opposite reasons. I believe that this strike and its termination has tended to shake the whole confidence of the public in the efficacy of our machinery for the peaceful settlement of disputes. I believe that it has tended to upset the very basis of our system of civilization, namely, respect for law. I believe that it has given the green light to those who want to show that they have the strength to strike and unwillingness to obey the law or comply with the machinery provided for peaceful settlement. It has tended, as Mr. Justice McTague said, to discourage the unions which have tried to comply with the law.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South was very fair in saying what the purpose
War Labour Board

of this strike was. He said that the strike was to protest against the holding of a ballot. I submit, Mr. Speaker, to you, to this house and to the people of Canada that that is not sufficient justification for holding a strike in war time. There was machinery available to be used; the brotherhood was already using it, and it should in fairness, in decency, as well as from the point of view of legality, have allowed that machinery to work.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South brought up the question of the provocative ballot and the action of the company in allowing that to be held. I would admit for the purpose of argument that there was room for criticism in that action while the matter was under advisement. But even admitting that, even if that' is well founded, then I say that it is no reason to hold a strike and tie up the traffic and transportation of the metropolis of Canada in war time.
We should look at this with all seriousness; we should recognize that a considerable number of unions have' already begun to move along the lines indicated by this settlement. We should recognize that, and I think we should appeal to them, appeal to employers and to labour alike, to recognize exactly where this kind of warfare is going to get us. There are just as patriotic men and women in the ranks of organized labour as there are in the ranks of employers, and there are just as patriotic employers as there are patriotic men and women in the ranks of labour. We all have to recognize that we are fighting this war for our very lives.
I would divide labour disputes into those which directly or indirectly affect the war effort, and those which do not, and any union which takes upon itself the responsibility of interrupting the war effort must have a very sound justification for it, if any justification is permissible. But that does not mean that we should allow industries to disregard grievances. It does not mean that there should not be the best possible machinery to dispose of labour disputes. Of course there should be that, and my proposals are these.
This development does create in a sense a new situation, and we should1 see the consequences and see that the people see the consequences of it, that employers and employees see the consequences of it, and try to rebuild the foundation of confidence and trust and respect for law. It is in very large measure a matter of morale and of information.

Last night I was with a number of people engaged in the production of munitions, and I asked them what percentage of the men working with them really understood the basis, the justification, and the necessity, for the wage ceiling and the price ceiling. They told me that it would be hard to guess-perhaps one per cent, perhaps two per cent. I do not know if that is the number or not, but I do know there is room for great improvement in the information that is given to all classes in Canada on some of these rather difficult questions-why, for instance, it is necessary to have the wage ceiling; why it is necessary to have the price ceiling; how labour codes work, and so on. I believe that there is need for a continuing process of informing the public by and of discussions so everyone knows, so that nobody can plead ignorance, and so that there is no possible excuse for irresponsibility of any kind.
The second suggestion I would make is this. Mr. Justice McTague yesterday in his speech implied that even he had some difficulty in construing the labour orders as a whole. I have not a full list of them, but I must confess that they are becoming hard to understand and to work together. I will mention, if I may, a few of them, some of which may now have been repealed, but that just shows how difficult it is to follow them.
P.C. 3495, November, 1939, which extended the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act to industries engaged in war work;
P.C. 2685, of June 9, 1940, providing for collective bargaining;
P.C. 7440, of December, 1940, which provided1 for a voluntary cost-of-living bonus and extended the application of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act;
P.C. 8253, November 15, 1941, which introduced the compulsory cost-of-living bonus and provided for the national and regional war labour boards; replaced by P.C. 5963;
P.C. 2442, of June, 1942, which appointed the industrial disputes inquiry commission which was amended by P.C. 4844, and 496;
P.C. 7307, of September 16, 1941, requiring a strike vote;
P.C. 629, of January 26, 1942, with regard to shipyards.
Then there is P.C. 689, and a number of others which I have not mentioned.
The time has come when it is desirable that all these laws should be worked together into a code and that that code should be passed on the floor of this house. These matters affect the people of Canada to such- a degree that

War Labour Board
they cannot be best dealt with by a series of orders in council. They should be the subject of legislation introduced and passed after discussion on the floor of this house.
The dispute arising in connection with the Montreal Tramways indicates that there is a positive gap in our labour legislation. I think the minister himself was conscious of that. On the Sunday he sent three telegrams putting forward constructive proposals, sensible proposals, proposals 'which he should have been able to make stick for a day or two at least. In order to implement the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, which is probably the only federal legislation which gave jurisdiction to the dominion government in this matter, there should be a provision for stand-still orders while a matter is under consideration before a board.
Finally, there is a further matter, in which I see eye to eye with my hon. friends in the far corner of the house. I do not see how we can expect labour to have a true sense of partnership in the war unless they are given a full measure of participation in all the agencies and instruments that we appoint for the conduct of the war. I support, on this, the remarks which have been made at various times from all parts of the house. We must recognize that this must be a partnership. And we must reestablish the one basis of dealing between partners, which is faith in each other's honesty of purpose and willingness to abide by the rules as they are made from time to time.
My hon. friend in concluding hi3 speech said he thought in the tramways strike the right side had won. I do not judge the tramways strike by that measure. What concerned me about the strike was that it tended to prevent the right side in the war from winning, and for that reason I thought it should be deplored.
If that decision-that strike and its settlement-is used as the starting point of a whole series of labour disputes, pushing here, pushing there, then they will go right through the price and wage ceiling and we shall see a situation which we have never seen before in Canada. If, on the other hand, we sit down now, look at the matter calmly, and take counsel with each other and think what is best in the interests of Canada, how best we can improve the machinery to secure the prompt administration of the rules we adopt to secure fair treatment for all, then this strike may be a warning to us. We have time to profit by that warning, and I have taken up the time of the house this afternoon to bring the seriousness of the challenge to the attention of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I have been asked to
say a few words in this debate, and I am very glad to do so.
The debate opened with criticism of Mr. Justice McTague, chairman of the war labour board, for having spoken recently on a labour matter in Montreal. I believe that on the same day, or on the preceding day, Mr. Cohen, another member of the war labour board, also spoke in Montreal. I have heard no criticism on the latter's speech, and I assume that Mr. Justice McTague and Mr. Cohen have equally the right to place their views before the public. Since they are entering upon a new service, it seems to me very proper that they should do so.
Of course the government had no knowledge of what either of these men would say in his speech; but I have read very carefully the report of Mr. Justice McTague's address, and I agree entirely with the statements he made on that occasion. Mr. Justice McTague has been appointed by the government to the chairmanship of a board of three who will be the supreme arbiters in labour disputes under the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), and it is the intention of the government to give wholehearted support to Mr. Justice McTague in carrying on the work of his office.
One thing he said, with which I entirely agree, is that the government had been all too patient. I think there has been a tendency on the part of one section of organized labour to place too much reliance on the action of the government in the steel strike as it may apply to future disputes. The government took action in the steel strike for a number of reasons. One was that it was reluctant to lose the production of the steel. That was one basic reason, and it arose particularly out of our being called upon at that time for a greatly increased output of escort vessels. Another reason was that the government realized that the steel dispute had been unsettled for a very long period, and it felt that the men had some cause for impatience in that regard. In any event the government did take action even though the men were out on an illegal strike. What is done is done, but I think there is no justification for a circular which came to my desk, as it happened, just before I came into the house. It is signed by R. J. Lamoureux, provincial director, U.S.A., C.I.O. I will read two paragraphs
All Sherbrooke steel workers are cordially invited to attend this organizing meeting of the United Steel Workers of America, C.I.O.
Come and hear how the union forced the Ottawa government to pay fifty-five cents per hour to labourers in basic steel plants in Canada.
War Labour Board

I hardly think that if the government had thought they were being forced to that .settlement, the settlement would have been made. The government intervened to straighten out a situation which seemed to require immediate attention. They did not do this because they were forced to do it; they did it because, even though it was an irregular procedure under the labour procedure of this country, they believed that special circumstances justified that action. Therefore I ask labour leaders throughout the country to use the existing machinery of government in settling disputes. We have never had such a complete system for the adjudication of labour disputes as we have to-day. In fact we have a labour court which will interpret the government regulations, not in a narrow spirit but, as Mr. Justice McTague said, in a spirit of equity and justice. There is no dispute in the field of labour that cannot be adjudicated by his board and the boards that operate in the several provinces. If labour attempts to short-cut local boards or the central board and tries to force the issue by an illegal strike, the weight of the government will be definitely in support of law and order, and the labour organizations will find that an illegal strike in an attempt to short-cut legal procedure will not help the situation.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: Will it work the other way, too?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: Yes, quite. It has been suggested that a strike vote is necessary to bring an application before a regional war labour board. That is not the case, as my hon. friend knows. An employer can bring a dispute before a regional war labour board, or an organization of employees can do the same.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: I said a conciliation board.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: Yes, but conciliation boards are hardly required in days when we have a judicial body capable of dealing with any sort of labour dispute.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: The steel workers had to go through that.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
As the machinery is to-day, I am sure that a strike vote is not required.
Reference has been made to shops laying off men. All hon. members will realize that we have been in the war now for three and a half years, during which period we have made a huge volume of munitions. We still require a huge output, and each day that output is growing, just as the number of men and women employed in the munitions industry is growing. Nevertheless we have reached the point where 
the requirements for certain types of munitions have been filled. That will be more and more frequently the case as the months go by and our output continues to expand. My hon. friend mentioned the National Steel Car plant employees who were formerly engaged in making 4-5 shells. The situation there is that we have in this country more than seven months' output of 4-5 ammunition, and that ammunition is not moving forward. We are told that the total requirement has been met and is at present in store in Canada. Obviously, with that knowledge we cannot continue to make 4-5 ammunition. My hon. friend may ask why we do not take these machines out and put in other machines to make other types of ammunition. The reason is that future developments of the war may make the manufacture of more 4-5 ammunition necessary, and it has been considered wise to keep that machinery in place so that we can resume that type of production when required.
An hon. member asked about the situation at the Angus shops and why we do not continue to make Valentine tanks. I think that matter has been explained to hon. members. The Valentine is a very useful tank, but it has become outmoded in all countries except Russia. It is no longer a first-line weapon as far as other allied countries are concerned. There was a considerable production of the same type of tank in Britain, and in a survey of the situation it was found that, by continuing her normal production, Britain could supply more Valentine tanks than could be shipped to Russia under existing circumstances. The question of continuing Canadian production was gone into fully with the authorities in Great Britain. We were reluctant to give up the production, because it was well organized and had been proceeding smoothly for a long period. However, it was the combined judgment that Valentine tanks in the required number could be supplied to better advantage from Britain than from Canada. We also had to keep in mind that our expanded escort vessel programme required new capacity for the production of components. All factors having been taken into consideration, it was decided to turn over the Angus shops to the production of ship components.
In the matter of the transfer of employees by selective service, an unfortunate situation occurred. We inquired of the management how many men would be displaced by the change in production, and I think the first answer was that only 100 men would be displaced. Some two or three weeks later we were advised that this number had been very

War Labour Board
greatly increased. Therefore there may have been some delay, arising out of that situation, in placing the men through selective service.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: Would the minister explain to the house why fewer men are required in the manufacture of these ship components? Would they not be using the full capacity of the plant, or is the work of a kind that does not require the full capacity?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: It is a combination of both. We cannot start in immediately making all the ship components that we will make eventually. There must be gradual expansion of tooling, facilities, and employment. We are going to make all the ship components we can in that shop. However, it may take time to gather strength, and I could not answer the question as to whether, when we are up to full capacity, we shall need all the men who were employed on the tanks. Different types of work require different numbers of men.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: The thing that puzzles me is that last October we were told that the production of tanks would be discontinued in March and that then this shop would go into production of marine engines. Now we are told that it may be months before these men are completely reemployed. It seems to me there has been delay in planning this transfer from one type of work to the other, and I think that is the main criticism.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I hardly think that is true. As a matter of fact we could not do very much until the tanks went out of the shop, and they went out only a few week ago. When the tanks went out, patterns for the new work, which had been prepared in other shops in the meantime in order to avoid delay, were moved in. In starting new production in a new shop you cannot start at full tempo; as the product comes nearer to completion, more men are required. However, we do need these men elsewhere and they will be transferred to other work.
My hon. friend spoke of shipyards. Perhaps he overlooked the fact that this is the most difficult time in shipyards, when the winter work is nearing completion and when no ship can be "launched from, the ways until the river frees itself from ice. It is probably the most difficult period of the year in which to expand employment in the shipyards along the St. Lawrence, but additional men are required in shipyards, particularly along the great lakes where there is a considerable shortage of experienced men. There is also a shortage of men for many types of work similar to that carried on in the Angus shops.
My hon. friend spoke of men making the statement that they could build six tanks a day
in the Angus shops but that they were held down to three a day. I would remind hon. members that the Angus shops are only an assembly shop for tanks. I suppose less than five per cent of the components that go into the tank are manufactured in that plant.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: What per cent of the component parts are manufactured in Canada?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I could not say offhand; perhaps about eighty per cent. If my memory is correct, the only imported component is the engine. There were a number of shops engaged in producing other components. We were asked to organize for a production of three tanks daily. We did that, starting back with every component shop, even the shop in the United States that manufactured the diesel engines. We organized completely for an output of three tanks a day. The fact that the Angus shops could have assembled six tanks a day, had they had the components, is not material, because we were organized for only three tanks a day. From the commencement of the production to the finish of the programme the average of three tanks a day, or eighteen a week, was held accurately. There were one or two delays due to components getting out of step, but the delays were always caught up and production maintained. An end-product shop cannot of itself step up production unless the whole line of shops behind it is stepped up in the same ratio. Usually the end shop, the assembly shop, has considerably more capacity than the component shops behind it.
My hon. friend spoke of the six-pounder gun made by Dominion Engineering. He said the shop could turn out one thousand guns a month, whereas it is turning out only four hundred. The reason is exactly the same as in the case of 4-5 shells. We were asked to cut down to four hundred guns a month, because we had caught up with the initial requirements for that type of gun. My hon. friend will realize that, when armies are being mobilized, there is great urgency to provide the initial equipment. After a time that is provided, every unit has the required number of guns, and then the production requirement depends upon the wastage, or in other words, upon how many guns are lost or destroyed in action. As action goes on, six-pounder guns will be required in certain numbers, but unless the action is very severe we shall not require a thousand guns a month from that plant, although in the initial stages it was tremendously important, in getting our armies armed, to-have that large capacity.
I do not know that I need say anything further on the subject, but I would ask all hon.
War Labour Board

members to do all they can to prevent labour disputes at this critical time. There are indications of the possibility of jurisdictional disputes in certain areas; that is a dispute between two rival labour unions. That is the most baffling type of dispute for employers or conciliation boards to deal with. The Montreal Tramways dispute is a sample; no demands had been made; the government was simply informed that in a few hours the men were going on strike. I hope that labour leaders will be particularly careful to avoid that type of dispute. If there is a question as to who is the bargaining organization for an industry, machinery is provided to obtain a just decision without a strike. That machinery should be and must be used.
I believe many of us think that because certain kinds of production are being interrupted, there is no longer urgency about war production as a whole. I should like to dispel that illusion. The requirement for ships was never so urgent as to-day; the requirements for aeroplanes were never more urgent; the requirement for radio devices and for a great number of types of equipment is just as urgent or more so to-day than it ever has been. The demand for raw materials of all kinds is as urgent or more urgent now than it ever has been. This is no time to relax, on the part of either management or labour.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Has anything been done by the minister's department or any other agency in Canada to enlist the men who are being laid off in a gun plant, say, and take care of them, keep them under supervision until they are reemployed? The reports I get are that these men are simply turned off, left to their own resources, not knowing where they are to be used. Is that impression correct?
- Mr. HOWE: That is not a correct statement. Before men are laid off, a report is made to the selective service organization, giving the names of the men and all particulars about their present employment. Selective service has the men in hand. Unless it is an isolated community I think it is only a day or two before the men are assigned to other work. I assure hon. members that the last thing that any of us want is to lose track of those men. We want to make sure they are employed, and employed in essential work.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: Is any provision made for giving the men an income while they are out of employment?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: The men of course have unemployment insurance. Every man is entitled to that.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
It is very inadequate.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apparently the recent tramways strike in Montreal is the motive power behind this debate. While I spent a day in Montreal during the strike, I do not intend to talk about -it other than to say, without entering into any of the causes of the dispute, either for or against the company or for or against those who called the strike, that I hope that as a result of that strike some clauses may be inserted in the industrial disputes provisions, if such clauses do not already exist, which would have the effect of preventing a recurrence of the situation which developed in Montreal. I should hope that if such provisions do not already exist, they might be introduced so that a thorough investigation and survey of all causes of a dispute might be made before any definite strike action is taken.
I am convinced that every man and woman in the house are as anxious as men and women everywhere that nothing should interfere with our war effort in any part of the country. It must certainly be recognized that a strike cannot do other than interfere with that war effort. When I was in Montreal during the strike I heard many people remark, " Is it not too bad that quantities of wrar munitions are not being made to-day, and were not made yesterday, owing to the inability of men and women to get to their plants?" Then, there were those who did go who had to walk so far that perhaps they were not able to do as good a job as they otherwise would have done. So that without entering into any of the causes of the strike may I express the hope that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) or the government will be able to find some way to ensure that such a situation does not recur.
I was amused when the Minister of Labour characterized as very bitter the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I do not believe the minister was in the house between 1930 and 1935.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Certainly I was.
Mr. AlacNICOL: Well, then he will remember that between 1930 and 1935 the hon. member for Vancouver East was much more bitter than he was to-day. Indeed I thought he was mild to-day, when compared with his former attitude. And I attribute his present state of mind to the fact that for the last eight years he has been sitting to the left of a sane opposition, one which at all times supports sound industrial and labour policies.

War Labour Board
I do not yield to any man in this house or out of it in my strong feelings of warm sympathy for labour. I have been one of them all my life, or at least until I retired from active work, and I am proud of it. That respect began in my childhood, because I remember well around 1887 or 1888, when I was a very young lad, my father was one of the organizers in the town in which he lived of that organization then known as the knights of labour, the organization which I believe was the forerunner of labour organizations in Canada to-day. I am happy that my father had a part in organizing one of the first labour unions in this country.
My observation in big industry through the years has been that labour unions have done a great deal to improve conditions in factories, and in fact in all aspects of labour. I will not now recite, as I have before, the many improvements in the life of the working man in industry, which have been brought about by labour unions. I have always admired the sound, sane labour leader. He has been a constructor; he has never been a destructor. He has been a builder; he has never been one who pulled down. Much good has come from labour leaders, men like John Noble in Toronto, associated with the American Federation of Labor, and like John Kelly of Montreal. Then there is a man in the Department of Labour who has been a stout advocate for many years of labour rights. I refer to Bernard Rose, K.C., of Montreal, one who has spent many hours in trying to adjust labour disputes.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: And Tom Moore?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, and Tom Moore. There is a long list of labour men. I had not intended to give names, because years have passed since I was in association with labour unions, and in that time many wonderful names have faded from my memory. I take my hat off to all sound labour leaders who have helped to build up labour in Canada.
On the other hand I cannot agree-well, I will not say that I cannot agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East, because as I said a few moments ago I have noticed a great improvement in him. I hope we shall not sit in opposition long enough for the hon. member to become 100 per cent right. Some day I expect we shall be on the other side of the house, and I hope when hon, friends who now sit opposite come over here they will also have a good influence on hon. members to my left.
My only criticism of him-perhaps I should say mild criticism-is that in his remarks he seems to class all employers in one and the same group. I have not heard him say much good for any manufacturers-although he may have said it without my hearing it. However,
I know hundreds of worthy manufacturers. There may be some in the group who deserve the criticism my hon. friend would heap upon them. For those who deserve such criticism I have nothing to say. There are employees and employers who might well be criticized. But the great rank and file of employers and employees are sound, Christian and otherwise, are God-fearing and good men.
This afternoon in conversation with the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding), who has been a labouring man all his life, working first in a junior position in the factory in which he was employed for so many years, and serving later as foreman, had only the finest words to say for the company which employed him up and down those years. That is the kind of company with which in my lifetime I was associated-and I have known many such companies. They need no defence from me. Their good works are legion. On the other hand I have not known the type of employer about which the hon. member for Vancouver East has spoken. I hope when he rises again to speak, even if he criticizes some he will have a good word to say for at least four or five, or possibly a hundred or so others.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member for Davenport that I did not include all.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that. That is a great improvement, due I am sure to the efforts of His Majesty's loyal opposition. I suppose most hon. members receive copies of the pamphlet published by the Dominion Foundries and Steel Company of Hamilton. I know this company very well because it has been my pleasure to visit it on many occasions. It is a huge organization, and I believe it now employs around three thousand or more hands. It takes a lot of money to pay that many men and women every two weeks. In the issues of this publication they never cease lauding their employees. They show that they are trying to do all they can to make the lives of their employees happy and comfortable and contented. I wish every company did this. The company with which I was associated a few years ago did this in a measure, but it did not get as far as the particular company to which I refer. However, it was on its way. Dominion Foundries

War Labour Board
and Steel Company of Hamilton i3 only one of many that I know of that are looking after their men.
The issue of this publication which I received this morning interested me very much. It contains a story about the fund for the employees of this company. It appears that the company makes a substantial contribution to this fund in addition to the contribution made by the employees. This fund was started five years ago when there were only 1,300 men and women employed. It might be noted that many of the operators in this company are women. The employees are of all races, and dt is interesting to read their names. Within five years this fund has grown to well up to $2,000,000. I got a great kick, I might say, out of reading what some of the men say about this fund. I wish I could repeat the Yorkshire dialect that is given, but I cannot. I will send this publication to the Hansard reporter so that it can be copied as it appears here. I am sure this will be most interesting to workers throughout the country. There is a picture of two workers who are discussing the fund which,' as I say, has now reached a total of about $2,000,000. This fund is administered by a committee made up of two men chosen by the employees, two chosen by the company, and a trustee. The benefits given to the employees by means of this fund are considerable. When I read of what is done for the men and women in this plant, I cannot help but hope that the same thing is going on all over the country. One man is named Sam Southern and the other is named William Greenwood. The first picture shows Sam Southern apparently looking at his book in which are recorded the amounts to bis credit in the fund. The caption under this picture reads:
"It's a bit a'reet, lad," says Sam Southern, looking over his fund book, "Wont Missus be pleased when she sees me creedit in fund!"
That is in real Yorkshire dialect. The next picture shows the two of them looking at the fund book, and the caption reads:
"Eh, lad. What does think abaht this, Bill?" he remarks to William Greenwood, "Looks as 'ow fund's summat talk abaht."
Hon. members will have to translate that to get the real meaning. The third picture shows Sam enjoying a smoke, and he says:
"Yeh, lads, a working man gets square deal 'ere a'reet. Got a job I likes, and me and Missus doan't need worry abaht future."
By means of this fund the workers are guaranteed sustenance when they are unemployed. That is as it should be. No man who has worked for a company for any length of time should have the least fear of want. Conditions 
to-day are different from what they used to be, and perhaps that is what the hon. member for Vancouver East had in mind. I can remember a company-I shall not give its name- which I would be ready to denounce if I were the kind of person who denounces things. I do not generally do that because I like to look at things in a broad way. In this case one man had worked for this company for thirty-seven years, and he was told to go. Another one had been with it for thirty-two years, and he was let out because he was too old. I believe the third man had been with the company for twenty-nine years.
I take the stand that no man or woman who has worked for a company for any such length of time, or even for a shorter period of time, should be let out -without the company being made to contribute to his care for the rest of his days. Legislation should be enacted to ensure that that is done. I met this one man who had been with the company for thirty odd years nine days after he had been let out. At that time he was talking incoherently ; his heart was broken, and he died three weeks after. It was a terrible thing to treat a human being like that. I do not think the same thing could happen to-day.
There is another angle about which I should like to say a word, something that should not be allowed in this country. I know a man by the name of R. Stuart. This man was an excellent salesman; he knew his business, and he was well known. One company after another bid for his services. They then agreed among themselves that they would divide up any contracts obtained. As new contracts came along, I am informed that an officer of one company would meet with officers of the other companies and they would decide that contract A would go to company B, and contract C to company D, and so on. This star salesman refused to be a party to any such agreement. The result was that he was discharged, and all the companies agreed not to employ him. That was nothing short of boycotting, and such a thing should not be allowed in this country. No man should be prevented from earr;ng a living if the opportunity is there. When things like that occur I agree to a certain extent with what is said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. However, such things do not happen very often. The standard of our business fabric has been raised up beyond what it was in times past.
There is something else about the Dofasco company fund which I think ought to be placed on Hansard. This circular states:
This Dofasco fund of ours is no longer in the experimental stage. Quoting Mr. C. W. Sherman, the fund trustee, in his annual letter to fund members-

War Labour Board
The report concludes what it has to say about the fund by quoting Mr. C. W. Sherman, the fund trustee, as follows:
Starting without assets five years ago, about thirteen hundred members have accumulated $1,633,438.49!
That fund has since grown to close to $2,000,000. Then he goes on to put questions about the fund:
What is the fund? What does it do? How does it operate? These and many other questions come to us frequently. The spirit of the fund is contained in the preamble to the fund agreement, and we think should be read again and again by every fund member.
Here is the preamble:
Whereas the "employees' are desirous of contributing to a fund that will enable them to save and help provide for their future.
I quote further:
"What does our fund do?" you ask. It is an incentive for the worker to save, and we are confident that we will find the majority agreeing with us when we claim that Dofasco men have been taught to save who previous to joining the fund never saved a dollar in their lives, for the purpose of providing security for the future.
They go further than that. They give their men an opportunity to advance. To stand working at a machine, either a boring machine, a drill, a lathe, a shaper or some other machine, eight to ten or twelve hours a day and doing it day in and day out is pretty hard work. I have seen it times without number. This particular company, and I know many others which do the same thing, runs a night class in connection with its plant where bright young men and the older men who want to advance have an opportunity to learn many other branches of the work in the plant. They can learn to operate other machines and in that way advance themselves. There is plenty to eat in connection with the night school, and they occasionally put on some little amusements. So that altogether they are a very happy family.
Not far from the Dofasco plant there is another great plant, that of the Bertram company. Most men and women in this building know about the Bertram company. Its plant is of tremendous size. I believe it is the largest machine manufacturing shop in Canada and perhaps one of the largest in the British empire. The head of the firm is a wonderful man. I have met him many times. He worked his way up from the bottom to the top. I refer to Mr. Henry Bertram, who I believe is now president. He is well advanced in years, being over eighty years old. I have often been with him through that plant, and
nothing delights that dear old man, if I may affectionately call him so, more than to go through the plant greeting the employees he knows so well. He will say, "Good morning, Bob-Good morning, Tom," and so on as he recognizes his old employees as he walks through the plant. His greatest pleasure is to tell you how long they have been with the company, and he will tell you that this one or that one has worked for so many years with the Bertram company. Many and many of them have worked for the company for fifty years or more. I remember one old employee, the late Geordie Turnbull, who had been with the company for sixty years. He worked there for some years after that. Geordie Turnbull just praised that company from morning till night. He was a great booster and lover of the company, and well he might be after having worked there for sixty years during which he rendered excellent service. He had a right to think well of the company, and the company had an equal right to and did think well of him.
In my own riding, not far from where I reside, there is a much smaller company, and it is only one of a. number such. I believe there are more factories in the riding I represent than in any other riding in Canada. I know many of them well and go through them at every opportunity I get. This one plant I have in mind at the moment is a branch of a United States company, the C. A. Dunham company. It would delight anybody to go through that plant. In the forenoon all the employees knock off work for fifteen minutes to rest and have tea, and the same thing occurs in the afternoon. Those employees all get holidays with pay and are all insured, and I doubt very much whether you could dynamite a man or a woman away from that plant. That is only one of many. That is the way it should be. In this enlightened age men and women working in industrial plants should be treated in the most human way, because it is tiring and monotonous to stand up and work at a machine all day long. I have worked on a machine myself for nine and twelve hours a day and I know what it is like. When you have to work at a machine for ten or twelve hours a day, a fifteen minutes' rest together with a cup of tea and something to eat, in the forenoon and in the afternoon is most welcome. It helps to take away the monotony of the work, and the day seems shorter, too, if you have a chance to advance. I had a chance to advance, and I improved it and did advance. There are many other plants I could speak of in the same way.
War Labour Board

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we are in the greatest war in the world's history, and this empire stands in greater jeopardy than ever before. At such a time every effort should be made by every one of us to prevent a possibility of strikes or lay-offs. Every effort should be made by every one of us to keep the wheels of industry operating to the limit. I might address a word to the Minister of Labour. If there are some obstinate employers who refuse to listen to sound advice, to an appeal to keep their employees working, it is up to the department to step in just as the department steps in when a strike is called by the working men.. The stand I take is this. We are all together. We all sink or swim together. We cannot swim if some of us are interfering with the rest of us working,. We cannot swim if those who are working are not receiving fair play. That is simply the golden rule, and I believe the golden rule is the one to be followed by labour leaders, by industrialists and by our working people, more than ever at this time when the empire's life is in jeopardy. If we all do unto others as we would have others do unto us, I believe strikes would be a thing of the past at least until after this war, and after the war some legislation should be brought in by the department that would ensure that before any strike is called, every avenue for preventing the strike shall be first explored with the object that men and women who want to work, and who should have work, Shall be given the opportunity to earn the most they can under the fairest conditions, so that they can take care as best they can of their wives and families and lay something by for their old age.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SPEECH IN MONTREAL OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I have had as long an association with labour as any other member of this house. I have been a consistent supporter of labour all my life. I believe in certain principles which we should follow in this, the greatest war the world has ever seen. The first principle is that the country should come first. The second is that the safety of the state and the promotion of peace in industry should come second. The war should be our primary interest, not secondary.
During the last war in the city of Toronto we had a number of large strikes. There was one in the police department and the street department, one in the post office department, several in industry, and there were several street railway strikes. I have always found the average labour man to be, on the whole, a sane and sensible citizen. We in the
[Mr. MacNieol.l
House of Commons are supposed to be together for the war, and not to use the war to promote our own political theories or policies.
On this, the forty-ninth day of the session, the war seeems to be in the background altogether, although the situation is most grave. Mr. Churchill has referred to it; Mr. Eden spoke of it in this chamber the other day; and to-day Mr. Knox, secretary of the United States navy, referred at Washington to the gravity of the submarine menace in the Atlantic. Up to the present our allies have never been able to get inside the German . defences on the continent. Mr. Churchill has aptly described the situation up to now as "the end of the beginning" of the war; and nobody knows what will be the outcome.
Yet, unless w'e win the war, there can be no collective security. To-day there are no labour unions in Germany, Italy or Japan.
We are seriously handicapped through lack of shipping. When you travel by railway today, along any right of way, what do you see? Big, heavy packing cases, and crates and boxes of munitions and supplies. Many of them have been on the ground all winter and are damaged through exposure, but we have neither, the rolling stock to advance them to the seaboard nor the ships to move them overseas to help our allies.
As I said, there are no labour unions in the axis countries. In considering our labour difficulties it may be useful to recall the position of labour in Great Britain before the war started. At that time the Labour party in the old countiy was divided into five or six groups. First, there was the Lansbury group, which would not fight for anything. Then there was the group led by Sir Stafford Cripps, who announced that they would fight for socialism and nothing else. Speaking at Bristol, he said:
I think we ought to warn the government that in no circumstances will we go to war. There is only one way we can make that threat effective, and that is to call a general strike.
Mr. Attlee, another labour leader, was attached to the League of Nation's group, who were ready to fight for collective security, but not for Britain and the empire.
The coming of the war united the labour party in the old country, and they voted by a majority of three and a half million votes at the Norwich conference in favour of a total war effort, without strikes. I wish we could pattern ourselves on that example. These people are right beside the war and they know what is happening. Mr. Eden reminded us the other day that the British House of Commons are not meeting in their old chamber; they are assembled in another place because of the bombing of Westminster.

War Labour Board
I believe we should model our labour-capital relations in time of war on the old country. Remember that there are demagogues on both sides; they do not all belong to one group. In the old country the safety of the state comes first, and they are comparatively free from strikes.
In Ontario, before the advent of public ownership, there were many strikes in the light, power and1 transportation industries, including the street-car systems, but under public ownership labour has had a better deal, shorter hours, improved conditions and higher pay, and in every way the system has been an immense success. Since the war began we have embarked upon what may be called public ownership of certain industrial plants, making them into crown plants. While it is true that in some places there has been a good deal of absenteeism, and in some instances improper labour conditions, yet the work done by labour in general industry, and particularly in munitions and supply, is one of the most glorious records of which Canada can boast. I hope that by no act of this house shall we cause unrest or work up a case for a general strike; and remember that these things have been said, not only in Montreal during the past month, but in other oities, suggesting a threat to summon a general strike. Well, are we in the war, or are we not? We shall have to decide that question. If strikes in Canada are not legal, why are we dealing with people who have been guilty of non-legal proceedings? Mr. Justice McTague, chairman of the national war labour board, to whom reference has been made to-day, has as much right to talk as Mr. Donaild Gordon had in Toronto yesterday about certain beef and other controls, and what should be done over the head of parliament while in session, and announce policies. I might say the same with reference to Mr. Grierson and a number of other gentlemen who are in charge of controls and sub-controls. They do not hesitate to announce, while parliament is sitting, important policies for the country; they are declared over our heads, whether we like it or not, by government boards of all kinds.
In the old country there was a debate a few months ago about the effect of strikes, absenteeism and certain other factors on the war effort of Great Britain. Some of the remarks which were then made are, I believe, quite relevant to the situation which developed in the island of Montreal the other day and to a situation which, unless regulated, may on May day, only three weeks ahead, assume national importance from coast to coast. I propose to read a few paragraphs from the speech of a very able friend of labour, who
himself rose from the ranks to become the head of a large business. I refer to Mr. Austin Hopkinson, the member for Mossley. He touches on the views of the fighting services. I may say that I have received many letters from our soldiers who are now in England and north Africa: they wonder what is the matter with us over here, and whether they are going to get adequate supplies and help; they refer to what their parents have told them about the packages of freight along the right of way of the railways, and about strikes and contemplated strikes. Mr. Hopkinson, speaking on November 19, 1942, said, with reference to the future of Britain's young men now in the services, what they will face when they come home:
From the purely economic point of view, what is being prepared for them after the war? I venture to say that one of the things which arouses more disquiet in their minds than anything is that there is a strong movement in this country towards having the life of every man and woman planned out by some superior authority, and there is no doubt they regard that with the utmost distaste. Again, there is a section of the community which we call "big business." Big business has nothing to do with legitimate commerce and industry, nothing whatever; it is a purely parasitic growth, living upon the lifeblood of industry and of the workers. It is obvious that big business, in collusion with the labour boss of the syndicalist type, is preparing a brave new world for these young men when they come home. Many hon. members will have seen a manifesto by big business recently. What did it mean? It meant that great monopolistic bodies will be set up in each industry, vested with statutory powers whereby they may crush every form of independent industry by making one great monopoly. By collusion with the labour boss they would always have a majority on the council for each industry and, by their statutory powers they could enforce their will upon everybody else. If I may misquote a familiar Latin quotation: "Solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant." That means, that these people would make a monopoly and call it peace.
That is not the first time we have had to fight against this sort of thing. Many hon. members will remember the "peace in industry" stunt of the late Lord Melchett some years ago, which was exactly the same thing as is being prepared in this country to-day. The idea was to set up large councils for each industry on w'hich the big monopolistic firms would always have a majority and, if they could work with the labour boss, as they intended to, would be able to crash out any chance for any of these young men who are now fighting for us abroad to make their own way in life and to contribute in due course their enterprise, energy and brains to the production of the common wealth of the nation. When I started in business forty years ago it was comparatively easy for a young man who had guts and enterprise to set up for himself, even without money, as I set up for myself, and make a success of an industrial concern. To do that is now becoming more and more difficult. If we allow big business and
War Labour Board

the labour boss between them to close up all the openings for enterprise and brains and energy, we shall betray all these young men in the lowest possible fashion.
That was his view of what would happen in the old land after the war as a result of surrendering somewhat to some of these socialist agencies. Let us get together and settle labour disputes until the war is won.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, while labour has accomplished many good things, I believe we should have some new future national policy for labour. We should not have two unions in war time fighting for mastery in Canada. They cannot both succeed. Sensible labour organizations and trade unions have been a blessing to every country,, but we in this House of Commons should beware that by any action of ours we make it more difficult for the average business man, municipalities and others to transact their affairs. Hon. members to the left claim to be the only labour party in Canada, but of course that is not so. The record of the Conservative party in Ontario and in the dominion shows a great many things done for labour. Hon. gentlemen of the party opposite sometimes have done a great deal for labour in the past, and during the last thirty or forty years Canada has given leadership and has been a pioneer in many labour matters. We have had splendid labour leaders, and I hope nothing will happen to spoil the magnificent record of labour up to the present time, through the fomenting of strife rather than "peace in industry" until the war is won. In these days the war effort should be paramount, because we do not know where we are to-day or where we shall be next summer, so that it behooves us as members of this house to do our best to encourage and promote peace in industry throughout the land.

Mr. Speaker I have addressed this house seldom during this session; but the subject which cropped up unexpectedly, as far as I was concerned, early this afternoon, is one to which I think I can make some modest contribution in order that the record may be kept straight, especially in regard to Mr. Justice McTague. In the past my district of Parry Sound has been famous for its fishing and hunting, as a sportsman's paradise. Some eight years ago it became famous in the matter of production, unequalled in Canada, in the Dionne quintuplets. It may not be generally known by hon. members that in my great district is one of the most efficient and most necessary war industries in Canada, the plant of D.I.L., situated at Nobel, which manufactures cordite and
TNT for Britain and Canada, and which employs more than 4,000 workmen. Before I put straight the record by giving this house some of the things Mr. Justice McTague said which, either wittingly or unwittingly, were concealed by the two hon. gentlemen across the way who attacked him, I wish to say that at that great Nobel plant the most splendid conditions prevail as between management and labour. They have gone hand in hand to the regional war labour board for adjustment of the wage scale. Some ten days ago the management and labour went hand in hand before the board again, in order to secure approval, as is now necessary, of the desire of the industry to permit workmen to have holidays with pay. The most splendid conditions have prevailed there.
I should now like to say a word about Mr. Justice McTague whose voice is of necessity silent when he is attacked in this house. As hon. members perhaps will recall, he was appointed to the bench in my province by a former administration, not a Liberal administration. He received advancement from the trial bench to our court of appeal at the hands of the present administration, and there he rapidly established a reputation as a great and distinguished jurist. For the last two years he has served this country while still giving part of his time to his judicial duties as a member of the court of appeal, working early and late, night and day. He has rendered magnificent service as chairman of a board under the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), dealing with difficult problems of depreciation and taxation, and in that connection also he has won a splendid reputation for fairness and integrity. Just recently he was selected as chairman of the very important national war labour board.
My hon. friends who attacked him in the early part of this debate selected one or two hand-picked sentences on which they endeavoured to condemn this great jurist in the minds of the members of this house and the people of this country. I thought the day had long gone by when that type of guerilla warfare was regarded either as parliamentary or as the right thing to do, even in peace time. I wish also to recall the fact that when Mr. Justice McTague was appointed to this new post a few weeks ago, the better element in organized labour from coast to coast in Canada, and I say that advisedly, were loud in their expressions of satisfaction, indeed their praise of Mr. Justice McTague as a man and as the new chairman of that board, and incidentally they praised the government for having made this appointment. I know of no

War Labour Board
responsible labour organization or man in Canada who voiced a single word of protest in regard to this appointment.

I was not aware of that. But now, after Mr. Justice McTague has given up in part his judicial position; after he has come to this new and difficult task, without reward of any kind except the reward that men get when they serve their country faithfully, we find that an attempt is made to sow the seeds of suspicion and to bring that noted jurist into disrepute, I suppose to serve some sort of purpose in the time to come. I deplore that. I wish to read a few extracts from the address delivered by this great jurist before a non-political club, the Canadian club of Montreal, composed, as was indicated, probably much more of those who would be employers of labour rather than employees. I point out to my hon. friends that this address could well be taken as a sane charter of tolerance, cooperation and give-and-take as between industry and labour, which might be blazoned across Canada, placed in the hands of every right-thinking union in this country and in the offices of every industry, because it is a magnificent charter. Let me trouble you, Mr. Speaker, with only a very few extracts from it which my hon. friends were careful not to give the house. That gentleman said in opening his address:
Your president when he invited me to speak here suggested I speak on the functions of the board which I now head, the national war labour board.
He then expounded the functions of that board. Surely, when a new board is about to deal with such vital matters, it is a splendid thing that before a non-partisan non-political club such as the Montreal Canadian club he should give an exposition of his conception of his duty as chairman of that board for the better understanding of people of all types in this country.
Mr. Justice McTague among other things- my friend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) quoted one of them [DOT]-said:
Generally speaking, the policy of the national war labour board is to construe liberally the order in council where the wage-earner in the low brackets is affected. As to the wage-earner in the higher brackets, generaly speaking we feel he must share in the sacrifice imposed upon us all by war and the government's economic policy.
Do hon. gentlemen quarrel with that as an enunciation of the privileges and duties of labour in this country during this war? Surely not.
Then in another place he said'-I cannot quote the entire address:
I believe in the principle of collective bargaining. As labour knows, I have never wavered from that position for years. Furthermore I believe that labour is entitled to have as bargaining agent the union of its own choice.
Do hon. gentlemen quarrel with that? Of course they do not.
Then he said:
It is my view that industry's day of being paternalistic and deciding by direct or indirect means just what type of union it will deal with h'as long gone by. . . .
Is that the language of a man who is there to serve industry only, or is it the language of a man who wants to see both industry and labour in this country united in the great effort in which we are engaged?
He said further:
Industry must do its share to see that the worker gets a fair deal under the law.

Well, it is in the record. The hon. member for Cape Breton South berated the press. He said that the press are always garbling things, getting things wrong. He was not complaining in regard to his own speech but about the report of some strike, I think. The chairman of the board is all wrong as far as lie is concerned; the press of Canada, or a portion of it, is also all wrong. Only because I am asked to do so I will put on record .what is reported in the Hamilton Spectator as the language said to have been used by the hon. member at a meeting in the auditorium labour temple on Sunday afternoon:
Churchill, said the speaker, hated Hitler and will fight him to the last ditch. "That's the most I'll say for him," he continued. "The people will have to get rid of the Churchills to attain their ideals."

That is the language of the hon. gentleman who wants to castigate the chairman of the national war labour board for his splendid speech in Montreal yesterday.
Now a few words more from that address, although Mr. Justice McTague needs no justification from me. I have read the sentence:
Demagogues, whether union organizers or politicians, must consider with care and caution the forces of mob rule which they may be letting loose in this country-letting loose not only on the country, but on themselves as well.
In concluding his speech, Mr. Justice McTague apparently had a foresight that was almost uncanny, because he said:
In closing, Mr. President, may I emphasize that I speak from a completely non-partisan viewpoint ... I speak in open criticism of no one. However, if anyone feels that the cap fits, he is welcome to wear it.
He should have said, If any two feel that the cap fits they are both welcome to put it on. And they put it on this afternoon in this house.
Mr. Justice McTague also said on that occasion:
I have always believed in the solid qualities of the average workingman. In this time of war as an individual I think it generally correct to say he meets his obligations as he sees them. When he goes off the track, it is almost always the result of agitational and opportunistic ambitions of leaders who place immediate personal and organizational ends ahead of the one big job which we must keep engaged in, if we are to maintain a way of life a deadly and ruthless enemy fights to obliterate.
Is that language of which any jurist should be ashamed?
It is important that labour should not be recklessly or needlessly disturbed in this very hour. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) sounded a warning to the house, one which I make bold in my modest way to emphasize. He said in effect that the present hour is one of grave peril. And those of us who have followed the history of U-boat sinkings in March, the complete records for which have not yet been given, are shocked and alarmed at the enormous quantity and tonnage of shipping the enemy has been able to destroy, chiefly in the Atlantic, in the month just closed. The aeroplanes we are producing- some of them I believe in Montreal-and the ships we are producing in Canadian shipyards are essential to combat that menace.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South is an advocate of ship production, and for that he deserves great credit. I do not wish him to think that I rise in the house to make any sort of attack upon him. On the contrary I believe he and the hon. member for Vancouver East have made some excellent contributions

War Labour Board
to our discussions in the house. I am not at all intolerant of them. But I do ask them- 1 do not warn them-to try to join with the saner labour leaders in the country, so as to put down dissension and the entertaining of suspicious ideas about men in places where they are serving without reward. Let us all cooperate, no matter to which party we may give adherence. Let us cooperate to build up, rather than to tear down, and to make our Canadian effort which, as Mr. Churchill has said, is already so magnificent, and one which is surpassed by none of the allied nations, even bigger and greater and better by endeavouring to have industry and labour unite, instead of trying to tear them asunder.
