speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) and have been particularly interested in his review of the situation in his own constituency. I was particularly interested in his statement regarding the productivity of that constituency, and especially his reference to the quintuplets. I noted particularly that when he referred to them he was pointing to his left, and I gained the impression that he might be referring either to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) or to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in an endeavour to give them some advice. I thought his reference was a happy one.
The hon. member for Parry Sound at the outset of his remarks said that no one in the house had sponsored the cause of Mr. Justice McTague, and that he thought he was in duty bound to offer a defence, in view of the fact that the judge was not here to speak for himself. I believe Mr. Justice McTague was ably defended this evening by the hon. member for Parry Sound. It is an astonishing fact that when anyone does say anything against a member of the bar there are always a great number of supporters in the house, men with high capabilities, who can and do meet such criticism. I do not know of a more clannish organization than that composed of men connected with the law.
I was interested in the remarks this afternoon of the Minister of Munitions and Suppy (Mr. Howe) with regard to labour conditions. I believe it is the desire of every hon. member, as indeed it should be, that there should be no strikes. Certainly that is my utmost hope. It is very disturbing to myself and, I believe, to hon. members generally when we see disruption in our production programme. But there is no use in hon. members laying the blame on the war labour board particularly, or on industry, or on labour. It is my opinion
that nearly all strikes are caused by government policy. Wherever one goes he finds that the root of the trouble is labour conditions, partly due to government policy, or to wage conditions which are definitely due to government policy. I suggest that if the government would go a little further and look into some of these conditions they might avoid a lot of trouble in the future, because certainly some of the conditions under which labour is forced to work, especially the rates of pay received by some of the lower paid workers, give cause for complaint. It seems to me the only way in which they can get relief from these distressing circumstances is either through advocating or possibly going on a strike. I believe the government would be well advised to look into these matters beforehand, to see if solutions cannot be found before strikes actually take place.
When the Minister of Munitions and1 Supply was speaking this afternoon with reference to the great number of men laid off at the Angus shops he referred to the construction of the Valentine tank, and stated-and I believe I interpret his remarks correctly-that the tank was outmoded, and that it was now going out of production. Away back last summer, when the committee was discussing this matter I pointed out that at that time the Valentine tank was considered outmoded, but hon. members on that occasion took great exception to my statement, and praised the tank. My information at that time has proved to be well founded.
The minister referred to the building of ships. The hon. member for Parry Sound has just indicated how urgently ships are needed, in view of the high rate of sinkings. I agree with him 100 per cent. But one of the things which alarms labour as well as industry is the fact that we are not producing as many ships as we could produce-and I say that advisedly. Hon. members who have spoken this afternoon have been very much concerned about shipbuilding. It will be recalled that not long ago' the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), when speaking in the house, pointed out that the Star shipyards in Vancouver had only two out of eight berths occupied. He predicted that before long even those two would be closed, through lack of work. Those are conditions which greatly concern hon. members.
I remember reading not long ago, I believe in the Vancouver Sun, that around two or three hundred men were being laid off from Vancouver shipyards, and the newspaper pointed out that they were being laid off because they had become so proficient in their
War Labour Board

jobs, and were working so expertly that they could now turn out ships with less labour in the same time. Anyone who is at all conversant with the situation there knows that statement was not true. That is not the reason why men were being laid off. I shall not discuss in detail what the reason was. It is sufficient for hon. members to know that not only in the Angus shops at Montreal or in the shipyards at Vancouver are men being laid off, but they are being laid off throughout the country. The result is that our war effort is not being carried on to the extent it ought to be. Let me refer again to some of the places that are having to face this problem. I have spoken a number of times in regard to the lay-off of men in Calgary. I have visited these plants personally and I know the concern of labour there. I also know the concern of the management. I may say that I have never visited a plant in Canada where industry was not as much concerned with increased production as anyone else and where labour was not just as much concerned as industry. In almost every instance both parties were concerned because they were not putting out as much as they thought they could put out.
When I brought up the question of the layoffs in Calgary the minister told us that one reason was the necessity of retooling, and he pointed out that the Calgary -Ogden shops had the largest order in their history. I should like to quote from a letter which I received since the minister made that statement. It is from a man in a rather important position in the Ogden shops, and he has this to say with regard to the tooding-up of that plant:
Now we know the reasons given for tooling up by Mr. Howe don't dovetail with practical experience and the majority of the men are fed up, anxious and probably very scared because we have had further lay-offs after the one you spoke of.
He then goes on to explain that the men are much concerned over the tremendous number that are being laid off in production plants throughout the country. The minister told us that these men would all be put back to work. I do not for a moment doubt his sincerity. On -many occasions I have said that I think he is doing a good1 job, but I think he is trying to do more than he should have to do. Another man who holds an extremely important position in the Ogden shops wrote to me after the discussion in the house, and in part he said:
I do feel that unless strong representations are made for a continuation of contracts we will be faced with the problem of further staff reduction.
That is an alarming state of affairs at a time when we are supposed to be in the midst of a war. The hon. member for Parry

Sound pointed out the great need for ships as a result of the number of sinkings that have occurred; yet we find that in Vancouver and all over the country men are being laid off. This curtails production. I am alarmed at this condition of affairs. I do not think we shall settle our strike problems or our production problems until this problem is overcome. These men are greatly concerned over the fact that in Calgary, Montreal, Vancouver and other places there are hundreds of men being laid off. This affects the morale of the -particular locality as well as the morale of the whole country. This, along with the low wages paid, especially to those in the lower categories, is bound to create disturbance, is bound to cause strikes. Until we overcome this condition our position will not improve. It is all very well to blame the war labour -board- or someone else, but that is not the real, fundamental cause. The real, fundamental cause is government administration and government policy. I appeal to the minister to look into these matters and correct them before further trouble comes upon us.	*

What we are suffering from to-day is the result of many, many years of opposition on the part of employers
War Labour Board

to labour organizations. It is unfortunate that when we went into this war, labour, which is so important, was found so completely unorganized as it was at the beginning of the war. That state of affairs must be laid at the door of the opposition which labour organizers have met with on the part of employers during the past year, and I have no doubt that the Minister of Labour has had his share of experience in that particular line. Consequently, labour to-day feels that unless it can organize itself while the war is on, it will find itself, when the war is over, in exactly the same position in which it found itself in 1918; and because labour was not organized at the beginning of this war, because labour feels that it must organize now, or it will have no chance when the war is over, you have all these efforts being -made across this country to organize labour.
Reference has been made to the large numbers of men that are being laid off. We accept the minister's statement that when it is necessary for an industry to change over from one production line to another there comes a period when it is impossible to keep all the men employed. Notwithstanding the minister's statement, labour all across this country is convinced that more could be done by way of careful planning and organization to see to it that when one job was finished another job was ready for the men to step into. That is the feeling of labour everywhere in Canada, that someone has fallen down on the job of planning and organizing the productive enterprise of this country when it becomes necessary every once in a while for a factory to lay off anywhere from 100 to 1,000 or 1,500 men.
There is another general complaint against production in this country. Wherever I meet industrial workers; whenever I speak at a meeting, I still find that a group of workers in our war factories will come to me at the end and make this complaint; I never visit a factory but I get this complaint, and I am confident that every member of this house is receiving letters day by day complaining of the fact that in many of our factories workers are kept idle because there is nothing for them to do. I am going to read a letter that I received this week from an employee in Massey-Harnis at Weston. I read this letter because it is typical of scores of complaints that I find wherever I go among industrial workers in this country. This writer says:
I have been working as a skilled mechanic in this plant for over a year and getting more disgusted every week. I shall not take a great deal of time, but on behalf of the people of the district from which I come I feel that I should express the uncertainty that obtains in that part of the country over the employment situation. I shall deal specifically with the situation in the one plant concerning which I have spoken here on former occasions. I refer to the cordite plant operated by Defence Industries Limited at Transcona, where, according to the answer placed on Hansard on March 29 last, as reported at page 1617, there were 4,485 employees in May, 1942, and where at the present time, ten months later, there are only 3,089, or a drop of 1,400. The last occasion of a lay-off was in the middle of March, and on March 19, on the orders of the day, I asked certain questions about this proposed lay-off. In reply the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr.. Howe) said, among other things:
This sharp curtailment is due to a sudden cutting off of export demand.
However, on January 9 of this year a notice was posted in the plant concerning a lay-off which was taking place at that time, a lay-off of 175. Another lay-off of 325 is taking place at the present time. This notice posted in January stated:
We would like to point out that our production schedules are governed by the needs of the armed forces. We have accumulated heavy stocks against their requirements and until such time as their demands increase the plant cannot be operated beyond the. proposed level of production.
There iwas another statement in the notice to the effect that it was hoped that peak production would be resumed in the spring.
At that time I sent a copy of the notice with a covering letter to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and he replied under date of January 14, saying in part:
The facts as stated in the notice are substantially correct, except that there is no information at this time on which to give any assurance that peak operations will be resumed in the spring.
War Labour Board

I do not need to read at any greater length at this point. I think what I have in mind is fairly clear; at least it was clear to those employed in the plant in January as it was in earlier months that the possibility of further lay-offs was ever with them. So that, when the minister made the statement that the curtailment on March 19 was due to a sudden cutting off of export demand, the workers wondered how to fit that in with the minister's words of a few months earlier substantiating the lessening demand for this product.
The result of all this is that the workers in that plant, who are drawn from all over greater Winnipeg, are uneasy as to the future of employment in that -plant, uneasy as to their opportunity to make a full contribution to production for the war effort.
I have in my hand a letter from which I wish to quote; and, bearing in mind the ruling just made by Mr. Speaker, if it is desired to have this letter laid on the table I shall be glad to do so. It is addressed to me from Mr. J. Paterson, president of the employees' union in that plant. It is dated March 20 of this year. He says in part:
The facts of the case are very simple: 325 to 350 men are being laid off starting to-day. The layoff will take place over a period of a month throughout most departments of the plant. The plant management simply claims that orders for cordite have been reduced and therefore men must be laid off.
But in the next paragraphs one discovers what is of still deeper concern to these men. He says:
There is a rumour that the plant may be closed down entirely. This rumour is borne out by a few indications rvhich at least point to additional layoffs in the near future.
The workers would like to know what the policy with relation to the plant is going to be. The present uncertainty and insecurity is certainly not making for improvement in morale.
Following receipt of that letter, I placed certain additional questions on the order paper with respect to that plant, one of which questions was:
Is it intended to continue the operation of the above plant for the duration of the war?
The reply by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, as reported on page 1617 of Hansard, was as follows:
This plant will be operated as long as the need for its product continues.
** I am not making the extravagant statement that I am receiving scores or hundreds of letters concerning this matter, but an average of at least half a dozen a week have come to me from workers in the plant along the same line, whether it is going to be continued, or whether it may be closed down at any time,

speechtext:
to the various councils which represent trade unionists, of a desire to play their part as equal participants in the struggle upon which we were entering. I have seen this early enthusiasm, this early desire and hope that there would be an opportunity for this participation dwindle off into disillusionment as a result of the rebuffs of one kind and another that have come. It is on account of experiences of that kind that one finds labour getting to the place where they feel they must fight every inch of the way. It is not that labour wants to do that, because labour, for example, does not want to strike. The working people do not want to lose the pay that is their loss when they are on strike. It is the necessity of showing their strength that forces them to take the action which has been taken on occasion.
These conflicts do occur at times. We must be realistic and admit that the interests of labour and management diverge at times. The tragedy to me is the fact that in a place such as this parliament of Canada there is not more of an attempt made to understand what labour is trying to do, more of an attempt madte to appreciate the aims and objectives of the working people of this country, more of an attempt made to see the things that they really want and to see them in their best light. On the other hand, we have explanations given of strikes and other things that have taken place. The explanations I have heard to date have been that labour has done things that were, not justified. Maybe at times things were not fully justified, but we do not live in a world in which things are absolutely right or absolutely wrong; we live in a world where we must learn the interests of each other, where we must learn to get along with each other. One of the first things that should be done by this house so far as labour relations are concerned is to try to understand what labour is seeking in the struggle in which it is engaged at the present time.
As I see it, there are two basic things in which the working people are primarily interested just now. First, they ask that they be permitted to play a full part in the production of the commodities necessary for the war effort, that their ideas as to the ways in which improvements can be made should be considered, that their ideas as to efficiency should have more effect on plans, and that their belief that all workers should be kept at their tasks should be put into effect. When the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) was speaking a few minutes ago the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. fMr Knowles.]
Howe) suggested that the things he was saying on behalf of labour were simply his own remarks which he would make on a public platform.
I shall have to speak for myself and not for the previous speaker, but I can say to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that it was not on the public platform; it was not in the form of questions asked at the end of our public meetings; it was in my office in connection with the work in which I was engaged before I came here; it was in my home; it was on the street; it was at gatherings of trade unionists, that this concern was expressed to me. Frankly, I have hesitated to use the stories I have heard about inefficiency and waste and failure to use men to the full. I have wondered whether the stories were exaggerated, and I wondered whether it might be regarded as not in the public interest to repeat such statements. The point I wish to make is that these complaints do not originate with us on the public platform; they originate with the workers who come to us.
If this debate is reported in full in the press and the workers see how we are rebuffed by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, in their minds they are likely to say, "What is the use in talking about inefficiency; we are just wasting our time. When anything is suggested we are given the usual answer that everything is all right, and that is the end of it." So far as I recall I have never made these statements at a public meeting. They have been made to me by workers time and time again. These people want to have some say in the management of our industrial process. They want to know that their ideas and their experience are being used. They feel that if this is done, industry will produce infinitely more than it is producing at the present time. That is the first concern of the workers of this country. It is a concern that they express, by no means with their tongues in their cheeks. They are showing genuine concern over the lack of full and all-out production, and they are being disillusioned when this is not achieved.
I believe the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) expressed the other concern of labour when he opened the debate this afternoon. That concern is for some measure of security after this war is over. The letter from which I read when I started my remarks indicates that this concern is felt by the workers in the cordite plant at Transcona, and it is felt by workers up and down this country. They want to know what will happen to them the day after the war ends. Labour feels that the time has come when it should

War Labour Board
be given, a real say in the planning and the managing and the conduct of the industry and economy of this country. So far as labour is concerned they feel that this is only an extension of the basic principle of democracy. They are not asking just for the right to send representatives to the various parliaments and legislatures of this land; they are asking for the right to have a say in the control of the things that affect their daily lives.
I shall not take up time to-night to discuss another parallel matter, but the fact is that the farmers of this country feel that they, too, have a right to take part in the conduct of the things that affect them in their daily lives. And so they have. Some day soon I shall have something to say about the necessity of the getting together of industry and agriculture on the prairies from which I come, in order to take advantage of the advances that modern science has made, such as the producing of rubber and plastics from agricultural products. Some of us feel that these things must be looked into immediately before there is further exploitation and the advantages of science gathered in by the few instead of being made available to the many.
I know there is the idea that the people in overalls, the people who punch a clock and work eight or nine hours and get pretty dirty and tired, then punch the clock again and go home perhaps too worn out to read much that is in the newspapers, are not the folks to run the life of this country, but that the people to run the life of this country are the big business men, the people who can come to Ottawa and make representations to the government as to what needs to be done for the industries they represent. After all, however, this country is founded on the principle and philosophy of democracy. We are waging a war at the present time with the whole idea of preserving democracy, and, as I see it, democracy in Canada means that the eleven-and-a-half or twelve million of us who are here, all of us, should have a say in the things that affect our daily lives all the way through. That will call for every bit of political democracy that we have at the present time, and far more. It will call for an increasing influence on the part of the farmers themselves through their cooperative organizations, and it will call for an increasing influence on the part of the workers in the things that affect their daily lives in and through a strong trades union movement recognized as a basic part of the life of this country.
I was pleased to hear the concluding remarks-naturally I took exception to some of his earlier statements-of the hon. member for
St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) this afternoon, when he asserted that the time had come to overhaul our labour legislation and the various orders in council affecting labour and to bring down a definite labour code that could be easily and fully understood. In my view that is a war-time necessity. It is what we should have now while the war is on, for the sake of more efficient production, for the sake of a better morale on the part of the workers, for the sake of security and some hope in the years that lie ahead after the war. In order to achieve all that we should have right now a labour code, one that would not just pay lip-service to collective bargaining as P.C. 2685 does, but would actually make collective bargaining the law, recognized as a part of the democratic set-up of this country.
In closing, it is my earnest hope that somehow we can get away, in this house at least, from the bickering back and forth between one camp and the other so far as labour matters are concerned, that we can rather think in terms of the working people and the farmers of this country as the real Canadians, the people whom we are here to serve. It is our job to try to understand them, and, in my view, if we seek to understand the aims and objects of the working people of this country, particularly as they relate to trade unionism and collective bargaining with full participation in the war effort, we shall find that their aims and objects are to a very large extent the aims and objects of the present war, and they deserve our support.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my -intention to take part in this debate, but I feel impelled to do so after listening to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Nose-worthy) and the hon. member (Mr. Knowles) who followed him.
I regret that a certain school of thought in this house see fit to put themselves forward as the champions of the working man. In the first place I should like an honest-to-goodness definition of who are the working men and the labour men in this country. Is it only those who join a union and are prepared to pay an assessment to some labour leader who derives a good fat living for himself from the payrolls of the working class? I think the farmer is just as much a labour man as any man who works in a factory. I am also prepared to say that the manager of a factory, who seeks to find a market for the products perhaps of union labour, is just as much a labour man as the worker in the factory. I believe that if we are to have unity in this country it is not right to segregate one small particular element of society. We must all go forward abreast together.
War Labour Board

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) at the conclusion of his address made a very slight reference to the farmer, and that is the only time I have heard the farmer's name mentioned in this debate. Let me tell hon. gentlemen that the code of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, if applied, would have a great effect upon agriculture because, if labour has an insatiable appetite and seeks only its own personal desires, that is bound to have an effect upon the price of the goods the farmer has to buy. In the post-war period, if labour will be reasonable, the greatest market labour can have for its products will be in the purchasing power of the farmer. Furthermore, what will happen in the post-war period will depend and is depending to a large extent upon the policies of this government to which some people strongly object, namely, the price control and labour freezing policies. It is the very same control that freezes labour and imposes price control which gives us increased purchasing power from the money we have to spend as consumers. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) pointed out a little while ago, everybody is favourable to price control except that little part of it which affects himself. We want to receive all the benefits, but we do not want to take our share of the responsibility. That reminds me of a fifth freedom. The Atlantic charter speaks of the four freedoms. But there is another freedom which our hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation would like to include as a fifth, namely freedom from responsibility. But you cannot have success without each and every man in his own particular station doing the thing he is best qualified to do, and I am doubtful whether the man in overalls is the best man to guide and direct the destiny of any industrial concerns.
The hon. member for York South made mention of his visit to Massey-Harris and was giving us his opinion of how it should be managed. That is the sort of thing I object to from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, because the fact of the matter is that if you will look over their records you will find that very few of them have had any experience in business or agriculture or many of the other things they discuss. We had in Europe a great paper-hanger, and he was excellent as a paper-hanger. It would have been a great deal better if he had stayed a paper-hanger.

The hon. member for York
South has taken a rather high and lofty plane, Let me quote from a newspaper report of a speech made by him at Toronto on September 28:
J. W. Noseworthy, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member of parliament for York South, told a party meeting in Eglinton riding last night that low morale in factories and in the armed forces is the "most serious defect" in Canada's war effort.
I am prepared to say that the group to which he belongs is doing everything possible to see that that morale is not elevated, by the very means to which I have referred'this evening. He has a good deal of sympathy for labour. So have I; I do not yield to anyone in a desire to serve labour. But let me tell him that ninety-five per cent of the people of the dominion come within the definition of "labour," and that he has no monopoly of the claim to serve the working people of this

War Labour Board
country. Moreover, it might be as well, if he wishes to be fair, that he should display some sympathy for those in the rest of society who are doing their best to see that labour is provided with a market for its product, which in many instances is confined to the capacity of labour. In this connection I might point out that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MaeNicol) made this afternoon a splended contribution to this debate.
I believe also that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) offered some suggestions which are far more worthy of this house and will do more to uphold the dignity of parliament and the nation than an effort to seize on little irregularities which have a tendency more or less to discourage people. The hon. member for Davenport spoke of the Dominion Foundries and Steel at Hamilton. I could mention several other important establishments in my own city of Brantford which are doing important work for the war effort. There are, of course difficulties; I believe labour can do a great deal to help solve those difficulties. Sometimes the executives need sympathy. I wfill quote again from a newspaper report of an address by the hon. member for York South, made at Picton on November 19. He said:
If you read the list of "dollar-a-year" men now on government boards you will discover that the list reads like a directory of directors. There is scarcely a large monopolistic enterprise in this country that has not a key man in a key position on some government board.
When this war ends big business in this country will be in the saddle and thereby have a stranglehold on our economic life such as never happened in this country before. Some of these "dollar-a-year" men at Ottawa wield far greater power than cabinet ministers or parliament itself. In fact, all the most vital regulations brought into effect since the war began have originated from the various control boards approved by the cabinet and proclaimed as orders in council without the knowledge of parliament. . . .
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if that kind of language is helpful? Hon. members in that particular corner are supposed to represent the intelligentsia of this house, but I am convinced that by their works they have not shown consistency to the principles for which they stand, as far as elevating the standard of life in this country is concerned.
I wish to draw attention to another newspaper item which appeared around the New Year and which rather amused me. I have noticed that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation claim to be the champions of the underdog and the farmer; they put themselves on the high and lofty plane of serving humanity. But I happened to pick up a 72537-122
Toronto paper one day just prior to the elections in that city. One column contains the slate of Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidates, and its choice for ward two for alderman is "ex-Alderman William Dennison". Mr. Dennison's card is at the top of the page. It reads as follows: (Advertisement)
In Ward Two It was Ex-Alderman Wm.
Dennison
Who stopped a milk price increase in 1941 Make him your alderman for 1943.
What chance has the farmer who follows a route with his milk cart?
It is interesting to follow in practice the code of ethics of our hon. friends from the time I have known them in this house. They are very anxious now to win the war. But I can well remember the time when they rose in their places in this chamber and lashed out against any military preparations. The member of that group and, possibly, the present leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Toronto were perhaps the two biggest factors in retarding the progress of any preparedness by this country for war.
Time is going on, and I have no opportunity of drawing attention to some other matters which were in my mind. But I could not sit still and listen without protest to this tirade of abuse of the Canadian people. If we are to have any solid respect for our country, the first requisite is a good respect for ourselves. No doubt there are many things in our country which are not good; but I take the view that, like a scandal which may happen in a family, sometimes the less said about it the better. I suggest the applicability of that policy to my hon. friends if they are sincere in the desire to make Canada the country it ought to be. It must be said that, so far, in the conduct of this war and in respect of what we have accomplished, -we do not need to accept very much advice from any hon. members on the other side of the chamber, except the group immediately opposite my end.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Perhaps it might be an old automobile that a parent in the United States is giving to a child in Canada. It is chiefly furniture, in cases where families have broken up their homes in the United States. Perhaps a parent has decided to close up his house and move into a flat. subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does the minister take any sort of affidavit from people who bring in these goods?

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: They have to be declared. Each case is dealt with on its own merits. There have not been a great many cases, but those which have come up have been difficult to deal with. We have had no way of letting them in up to the present time, whereas we would have been able to let them in if they had been left by a will. That is why this amendment has been brought in. Care is always taken to see that the government is not defrauded in entries of that sort.

INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
There seems to be a good deal of uncertainty as to the exact meaning of this paragraph; I am not sure that I understand it myself, but I am sure the minister will be able to give a clear answer.
It now reads:
That in respect of the taxation year 1942 the income tax liability, of taxpayers other than corporations, under subsection 1 of section 9 of the Income War Tax Act-
Here is the part on which I am mixed up.
-in respect of earned income and in respect of investment income up to $3,000. . . .
Does the S3,000 mean the combination of the two, or does it mean the earned income by itself plus $3,000 of unearned income or investment income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: The latter is the correct meaning.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: May I suggest to you with great deference, Mr. Chairman, that in connection with these resolutions which are to be dealt with by the committee, you read them in full. Otherwise members of the committee have not a very good opportunity to deal with them before someone asks that they be carried. They are not very long, and I think it would help the committee if that were done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: Can we carry this?

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: Well, I should think not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
I was afraid not. This is very important. This resolution provides for relief from overhanging income tax debt through forgoing one-half of the tax liability for 1942 on all earned income, and investment income up to $3,000. It enables the individual to get on a current basis and to pay the tax as it accrues.
Prior to the budget those advocating the adoption of the pay-as-you-earn system had emphasized the tax difficulties facing the person who, for example, joined the armed forces, lost his job or retired from active life to live on a pension. These difficulties will be wiped out by the provisions of this resolution. I feel that I should call attention to this point because, since the budget, while there has been a certain amount of criticism of the income tax provisions both in this house and in the press, there seems to have been little if any recognition of the very far-reaching benefits which flow from this tax-forgiveness provision.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: No one could believe it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
It has been said that the adoption of the pay-as-you-earn system in the form proposed has been used as a method of putting additional burdens on the taxpayers of Canada without raising tax rates, and it has been argued that there should have been a forgiveness of two-thirds rather than one-half of the tax liability. The fact of the matter is that there was no one percentage which would fit all cases. It is true there were only four months of deductions in 1942 of the liability under normal and scheduled tax. But what most people overlook is the fact that the national defence tax was deducted for the full eight months prior to last September, and that national defence tax collected at the source also was in satisfaction of 1942 tax liability. The result of these two sets of deductions is that some taxpayers by December 31, 1942, would have had more than half their 1942 tax already paid in the form of deductions. To forgive a higher percentage than 50 per cent would have meant credits or refunds to this group comprising hundreds of thousands of persons, and the effect would have been in
Income War Tax

many cases to lower their tax for 1943 as compared with 1942. It is true that above certain levels of income, and depending upon other factors, the 50 per cent forgiveness will mean that there will be a remaining tax liability for 1942 to be paid during the current year along with the current tax for 1943. In these cases an additional burden will have been imposed as a result of the change over to the pay-as-you-earn system. However, in recognizing this additional burden, one should at the same time point out the advantage to all taxpayers of being on a current basis.
It might be well if I give some examples of the amount of 1942 taxes still to be paid after the 50 per cent forgiveness. For example, a single person earning $2,000 will have $27 to make up in respect of 1942, if he had full savings offsets; he would have $59 to make up if he had no offsets. A married man with no dependents who earns $2,000 in 1942 will have only $2 to make up if he had complete offsets; he will have $43 to make up if he had no offsets. A married man with two dependents who earned $2,000 in 1942 will have overpaid his tax by $5 if he had complete offsets, while if he had no offsets he would still have $17 to pay after the 50 per cent forgiveness.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: If he has paid $5 more than his 1942 tax, does he get a credit on 1943?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
He is, I think, entitled to a refund. The committee will readily see that if, for example, two-thirds of the tax for 1942 had been forgiven there would have been substantial refunds in all the cases I have mentioned where there were full savings offsets.
As a general rule, the lower income groups were more nearly paid up on 1942 tax by December 31 than were the higher income groups. But I should like to dispel the idea that even so the cash required to be put up in 1943 will be much greater than the cash that had to be put up in 1942 by the salaried class.
For purposes of illustration I shall take a married person with two dependents and shall dssume that on the level of income of which I am speaking there will be complete offsets against savings requirements. In the case of such persons receiving a salary of $5,000 the additional cash to be found in 1943 amounts to $143, or about $12 a month. The $10,000 man would only have to put up $67 more in 1943 than he did in 1942. In the case of the $20,000 man the additional tax to be found in 1943 is only $316. I suggest that those who feel that they are being penalized under the requirements for 1943 should carefully examine
(Mr. Hsley.]
these comparisons I have made and reexamine their nosition as compared with what it was in 1942.
That I think will be sufficient to open the discussion on the matter. I do not know that it is altogether creditable for the government to be arguing that they have not imposed greater burdens or very much greater burdens. We need to get as much money as we can, and I think the fact that we shall this year collect from the people of Canada, if our estimates are accurate, $443,000,060 more than we did in the fiscal year just closed is about right, I think it is about in keeping with what we should expect the people to do. We are raising our total expenditures very considerably; the total expenditures for government purposes will be $5,500,000,000 according to our estimates, and we ought, it seems to me, to raise about fifty per cent of that by taxation. And that we aim to do this year, including the refundable tax. I would feel better if we could raise fifty per cent outside of the refundable tax, but I am doubtful whether we should raise our taxes much higher than they are.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
I think one mistake the minister made in connection with this from a public relations point of view is that when the budget was brought down it should have been made clearer that some sections of our taxpayers would be obliged to pay in 1943 a higher tax than they had to pay in 1942. _My personal exxperience in talking to various people from time to time, not large taxpayers but the average run of the mill taxpayer, was that he took from the general spirit of the budget speech that he would have something less to pay, or at least no more to pay in 1943 than he did in 1942. It may be that in the technical analysis of the whole situation it may be clarified in the minds of a good many. Nevertheless there were a great many people who felt that there was some forgiveness of an immediate cash character, and finally when the matter was more fully explained they found that they had to reorient their thought in that respect. I am not for a moment arguing in favour of lower taxation with the situation of such an urgent character; but on the other hand if you lead the thought of the public into channels where they think there has been some revision downward, it becomes more difficult for them, to reorient their position when they find out the whole situation. I know the minister was pressed for time, and I know that on a budget speech every point cannot be covered exactly and every reaction of the public cannot be anticipated. But if the minister had to do it again I feel sure he would make clearer to the public exactly what

the situation was with respect to the 1943 impost. That is one of the criticisms I have heard, and I am passing it on to the minister. It is perhaps too late to do anything about it now, but I think he ought to know the reaction that occurred in some classes.

speechtext: No. I follow these things closely, and I know the public reaction very well. This year the reverse was the case; the immediate reaction was that quite a lot had been handed to the public, and then on examination it wras found that not so much was handed to the public after all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: I certainly do.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: The minister is much more frank about it than the Prime Minister is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
I do not know any reason why I should not say it. But what I wish to say is that the budget speech of last year was strictly accurate in every way, and so was the budget speech of this year. If anyone will read last year's budget speech or this year's budget speech he will find no misplaced emphasis. He will find nothing misleading and nothing inaccurate, either in general or in particular, in either of the speeches.
But the manner in which they strike the public is something one cannot gauge in advance. It depends largely upon how they are reported, and depends upon the conception those who write them up may have. It depends also upon intangible factors which cannot be gauged. I am not to blame for any misapprehensions about either last year's or this year's budget.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: I thought my criticism was pretty mild.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes; it was mild, and I was going to acknowledge that it was mild.

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

subtopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

I just wished to make a little speech on the most interesting of all subjects, namely public reaction.
